source: To combat COVID-19,  clinicians and scientists all need to digest the vast amount of relevant biomedical knowledge in literature to understand the disease mechanism and the related biological functions. We have developed a novel and comprehensive knowledge discovery framework, COVID-KG, which leverages novel semantic representation and external ontologies to represent text and images in the input literature data, and then performs various extraction components to  extract fine-grained multimedia knowledge elements (entities, relations and events)  . We then exploit the constructed multimedia KGs for question answering and report generation, using drug repurposing as a case study. Our framework also provides detailed contextual sentences, subfigures and knowledge subgraphs as evidence.
ref: To fight COVID-19, clinicians and scientists need to absorb the vast amount of relevant biomedical research to understand how the disease works and which biological functions are involved. We developed COVID-KG, a new, comprehensive knowledge discovery framework. It uses new semantic representations and external ontologies to represent text and images from research literature, then extracts detailed multimedia knowledge elements: entities, relations, and events. Using drug repurposing as a case study, we use the resulting multimedia knowledge graphs to answer questions and generate reports. The framework also provides detailed contextual sentences, subfigures, and knowledge subgraphs as evidence.

source: This study explores the time-varying structure of market efficiency on the prewar Japanese stock market based on Lo's (2004) adaptive market hypothesis (AMH). In particular, we measure the time-varying degree of market efficiency using new datasets of the stock price index estimated by Hirayama (2017a,b, 2018, 2019a  ). The empirical results show that (1) the degree of market efficiency in the prewar Japanese stock market varied with time and that its variation corresponded with major historical events, (2) Lo's (2004)  AMH is supported in the prewar Japanese stock market, (3) the difference in market efficiency between the old /new TSE shares and the EQPI depends on the manner in which the price index is constructed, and (4) the price control policy beginning in the early 1930s suppressed price volatility and improved market efficiency.
ref: This study uses Lo’s (2004) adaptive market hypothesis (AMH) to examine how market efficiency changed over time in Japan’s prewar stock market. We measure these changes using new stock price index datasets estimated by Hirayama (2017a, 2017b, 2018, 2019a). The results show that (1) market efficiency varied over time and changed with major historical events; (2) the evidence supports Lo’s (2004) AMH in Japan’s prewar stock market; (3) differences in market efficiency between old/new TSE shares and the EQPI depend on how the price index is constructed; and (4) the price control policy introduced in the early 1930s reduced price volatility and improved market efficiency.

source: We design a homotopy continuation algorithm  for finding real zeros of sparse polynomial systems. Our algorithm builds on a well-known geometric deformation process, namely Viro's patchworking method. The algorithm operates entirely over the real numbers and tracks the optimal number of solution paths. In exchange, the algorithm is not universally applicable : It works for polynomial system with coefficients satisfying certain concavity conditions . More precisely, it requires the given polynomial system to be located in the unbounded components of the complement of the underlying A-discriminant amoeba. A preliminary implementation of an example from the literature suggests practical performance of the algorithm.
ref: We design a homotopy continuation algorithm to find real zeros of sparse polynomial systems. It builds on Viro’s patchworking method, a well-known geometric deformation process. The algorithm works entirely with real numbers and tracks the optimal number of solution paths. However, it does not apply to every polynomial system. It works only for systems whose coefficients meet certain concavity conditions. More precisely, the given system must lie in an unbounded component of the complement of the underlying A-discriminant amoeba. A preliminary implementation of an example from the literature suggests that the algorithm performs well in practice.

source: Liquid-liquid phase separation occurs not only in bulk liquid, but also on surfaces. In physiology, the nature and functions of condensates on cellular structures remain unexplored. Here, we study how the condensed protein TPX2 behaves on microtubules to initiate branching microtubule nucleation, which is critical for spindle assembly in eukaryotic cells. Using fluorescence, electron, and atomic force microscopies and hydrodynamic theory, we show that TPX2 on the microtubule URLanizes per the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, like dew drops patterning a spider web. After uniformly coating microtubules, TPX2 forms regularly spaced droplets from which branches nucleate.  TPX2 concentration tunes droplet spacing . A stochastic model shows that droplets make branching nucleation more efficient by confining the space along the microtubule where multiple necessary factors colocalize to nucleate a branch.
ref: Liquid-liquid phase separation happens both in bulk liquids and on surfaces. In living cells, the nature and roles of condensates on cellular structures remain unexplored. We study how condensed TPX2 protein behaves on microtubules to start branching microtubule nucleation, a process critical to spindle assembly in eukaryotic cells. Using fluorescence, electron, and atomic force microscopy and hydrodynamic theory, we show that TPX2 organizes on microtubules through the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, much like dew drops on a spider web. TPX2 first coats microtubules evenly, then forms regularly spaced droplets from which branches nucleate. The TPX2 concentration controls the spacing between droplets. A stochastic model shows that droplets make branching nucleation more efficient by limiting the region along the microtubule where several required factors come together to nucleate a branch.

source: We propose a general framework for measuring frequency dynamics of connectedness in economic variables based on spectral representation of variance decompositions . We argue that the frequency dynamics is insightful when studying the connectedness of variables as shocks with heterogeneous frequency responses will create frequency dependent connections of different strength that remain hidden when time domain measures are used. Two applications support the usefulness of the discussion, guide a user to apply the methods in different situations, and contribute to the literature with important findings about sources of connectedness. Giving up the assumption of global stationarity of stock market data and approximating the dynamics locally , we document rich time-frequency dynamics of connectedness in US market risk in the first application.
ref: We propose a general framework for measuring how connections among economic variables change across frequencies, using the spectral representation of variance decompositions. Frequency dynamics can reveal useful information because shocks with different frequency responses create connections whose strength varies by frequency. Time-domain measures hide these differences. Two applications show the value of this approach, guide users in applying the methods in different settings, and add important findings about the sources of connectedness to the literature. In the first application, we drop the assumption that stock market data are globally stationary and instead approximate their dynamics locally. We document complex changes in US market risk connectedness across time and frequency.

source: In this paper we present a  mathematical model of tripartite synapses, where astrocytes mediate information flow from the pre-synaptic to the post-synaptic neuron . The model consists of a pre-synaptic bouton, a post-synaptic dendritic spine head , a synaptic cleft and a perisynaptic astrocyte controlling Ca2+ dynamics inside the synaptic bouton. This in turn controls glutamate release dynamics in the cleft. As a consequence of this, glutamate concentration in the cleft has been modeled, in which glutamate reuptake by astrocytes has also been incorporated. Finally, dendritic spine head dynamics has been modeled. As an application, this model clearly shows synaptic potentiation in the hippocampal region, i.e., astrocyte Ca2+ mediates synaptic plasticity, which is in conformity with the majority of the recent findings   .
ref: This paper presents a mathematical model of tripartite synapses in which astrocytes mediate information flow from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron. The model includes a presynaptic bouton, a postsynaptic dendritic spine head, a synaptic cleft, and a perisynaptic astrocyte that controls Ca2+ dynamics in the synaptic bouton. These Ca2+ dynamics control glutamate release in the cleft. The model therefore describes glutamate concentration in the cleft and includes glutamate reuptake by astrocytes. It also describes the dynamics of the dendritic spine head. When applied to the hippocampal region, the model clearly shows synaptic potentiation: astrocyte Ca2+ mediates synaptic plasticity, consistent with most recent findings.

source: To resolve these difficulties. we developed CytoITMprobe, a  Cytoscape plugin. CytoITMprobe  provides access to ITM Probe either through a web server or locally. The input, consisting of  desired origins and/or destinations of information and a dissipation coefficient, is specified through a query form. The results are shown as a subnetwork of significant nodes and several summary tables. Users can control the composition and appearance of the subnetwork . Saving results as node and network attributes, CytoITMprobe allows Cytoscape users to manipulate and visualize context-specific information in a manner more flexible than its web predecessor . It also enables seamless integration of ITM Probe results with other Cytoscape plugins having complementary functionality for data analysis.
ref: To address these problems, we developed CytoITMprobe, a Cytoscape plugin. CytoITMprobe provides access to ITM Probe through either a web server or a local installation. Users enter the desired origins and/or destinations of information and a dissipation coefficient in a query form. The plugin displays the results as a subnetwork of significant nodes and several summary tables. Users can control the subnetwork’s content and appearance. CytoITMprobe saves results as node and network attributes, allowing Cytoscape users to manipulate and visualize context-specific information more flexibly than they could with its web predecessor. It also integrates ITM Probe results seamlessly with other Cytoscape plugins that offer complementary data-analysis functions.

source: We study how effectively a group of rational agents learns from repeatedly observing each others' actions. We find that , in the long-run, observing discrete actions of others is significantly less informative than observing their private information : only a fraction of the private information is transmitted . We study how this fraction depends on the distribution of private signals. In a largesociety, where everyone's actions are public, this fraction tends to zero, i. e., only a vanishingly small share of the information is aggregated .  We identify groupthink as the cause of this failure of information aggregation : As the number of agents grows, the actions of each individual depend more and more on the past actions of others, thus revealing less private information .
ref: We study how well a group of rational agents learns by repeatedly observing one another’s actions. We find that, in the long run, observing others’ discrete actions provides far less information than observing their private information: only a fraction of that private information is passed on. We examine how this fraction depends on the distribution of private signals. In a large society where everyone’s actions are public, the fraction approaches zero, meaning that the group combines only a vanishingly small share of the information. We identify groupthink as the cause: as the number of agents grows, each person’s actions depend increasingly on others’ past actions and therefore reveal less private information.

source: We propose a new approach to mixed-frequency regressions in a high-dimensional environment that resorts to Group Lasso penalization and Bayesian techniques for estimation and inference. To improve the sparse recovery ability of the model , we also consider a Group Lasso with a spike-and-slab prior. Penalty hyper-parameters governing the model shrinkage are automatically tuned via an adaptive MCMC algorithm.  Simulations show that the proposed models have good selection and forecasting performance  , even when the design matrix presents high cross-correlation. When applied to  U.S. GDP data, the results suggest that financial variables may have some, although  limited, short-term predictive content.
ref: We propose a new approach to high-dimensional mixed-frequency regressions that uses Group Lasso penalties and Bayesian methods for estimation and inference. To improve the model’s ability to recover sparse signals, we also consider Group Lasso with a spike-and-slab prior. An adaptive MCMC algorithm automatically tunes the penalty hyperparameters that control model shrinkage. Simulations show that the proposed models select variables and forecast well, even when the design matrix has high cross-correlation. Applied to U.S. GDP data, the models suggest that financial variables may have some, though limited, short-term predictive value.

Using the Wang-Landau algorithm Phys. Rev. ref: We present a theoretical study of how chaperones help small proteins fold. We describe the proteins with an effective potential model that uses Ramachandran angles as degrees of freedom. We model the chaperonin cage with an external confining potential that can also account for hydrophobic and hydrophilic effects inside the cavity. Using the Wang–Landau algorithm [Phys. Rev. Lett. 86, 2050 (2001)], we calculate the density of states, g(E), and analyze in detail the thermodynamic properties of confined proteins at different cage sizes. We show that confinement by the chaperone sharply reduces the phase space available to the protein, leading to much faster folding.

source: In the 1850s the term 'Aryan' was adopted as a racial category by French writer Arthur de Gobineau, who, through the later works of Houston Stewart Chamberlain, influenced the Nazi racial ideology. Under Nazi rule (19331945), the term applied to the inhabitants of Germany of non-Jewish origin; 'non-Aryans ' were discriminated against , then the target of systematic mass killings known as the Holocaust. The atrocities committed in the name of Aryanist supremacist ideologies have led academics to avoid the term 'Aryan', which has been replaced in most cases by 'Indo-Iranian', with only the South Asian branch still being called 'Indo-Aryan'.
ref: In the 1850s, French writer Arthur de Gobineau adopted “Aryan” as a racial category. Through the later work of Houston Stewart Chamberlain, Gobineau influenced Nazi racial ideology. Under Nazi rule (1933–1945), the term described non-Jewish inhabitants of Germany. The Nazis discriminated against “non-Aryans” and then targeted them in the systematic mass killings known as the Holocaust. Because of the atrocities committed in the name of Aryan supremacist ideologies, academics have largely replaced “Aryan” with “Indo-Iranian.” Only the South Asian branch is still called “Indo-Aryan.”

source: This paper derives a generalization of the Granger-Johansen Representation Theorem valid for H-valued autoregressive (AR) processes , where H is an infinite dimensional separable Hilbert space, under the assumption that 1 is an eigenvalue of finite type of the AR operator function and that no other non-zero eigenvalue lies within or on the unit circle. A necessary and sufficient condition for integration of order d=1,2,\dots is given in terms of the decomposition of the space H into the direct sum of d+1 closed subspaces \tau_h, h=0,%DIFDELCMD < \dots%%% , d, each one associated with components of the process integrated of order h.
ref: This paper generalizes the Granger-Johansen Representation Theorem to H-valued autoregressive (AR) processes, where H is an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space. It assumes that 1 is a finite-type eigenvalue of the AR operator function and that no other nonzero eigenvalue lies within or on the unit circle. It gives a necessary and sufficient condition for integration of order d = 1, 2, … by decomposing H into the direct sum of d + 1 closed subspaces τ_h, h = 0, …, d, each associated with process components integrated of order h.

source: Knowledge graphs (KGs) have helped neural-symbolic models improve performance on various knowledge-intensive tasks, like question answering and item recommendation. By using attention over the KG, such  models can also "explain" which KG information was most relevant for making a given prediction. In this paper, we question whether these models are really behaving as we expect. We demonstrate that, through a reinforcement learning policy (or even simple heuristics), one can produce deceptively perturbed KGs  which maintain the downstream performance of the original KG while significantly deviating from the original  semantics and structure. Our findings raise doubts about KG-augmented models' ability to leverage KG information and provide plausible explanations.
ref: Knowledge graphs (KGs) have improved neural-symbolic models on knowledge-intensive tasks such as question answering and item recommendation. By focusing attention on parts of a KG, these models can also “explain” which information mattered most to a prediction. We question whether the models actually behave as expected. We show that a reinforcement learning policy—or even simple rules—can create misleadingly altered KGs that preserve the original KG’s downstream performance while differing greatly in meaning and structure. These findings cast doubt on whether KG-augmented models can use KG information and provide plausible explanations.

source: We present a novel machine learning architecture for classification suggested by experiments on the insect olfactory system . The network separates odors via a winnerless competition network, then classifies objects by projection into a high dimensional space where a support vector machine provides more precision in classification. We build this network using biophysical models of neurons with our results showing high discrimination among inputs and exceptional robustness to noise. The same circuitry accurately identifies the amplitudes of mixtures of the odors on which it has been trained .
ref: We present a new machine learning architecture for classification, inspired by experiments on the insect olfactory system. The network separates odors through winnerless competition, then projects objects into a high-dimensional space, where a support vector machine classifies them more precisely. We built the network with biophysical neuron models. Our results show that it distinguishes inputs well and is exceptionally robust to noise. The same circuitry accurately identifies the amplitudes of mixtures of the odors it was trained on.

source: The intuition on risk is based on two main concepts: loss and variability. In this paper  we present a composition of risk and deviation measures, which capt these two concepts. Based on the proposed Limitedness axiom, we prove that this composition is a coherent, convex or co-monotone risk measure, conform properties of the two components . We also provide examples of known and new risk measures constructed under this framework , in order to highlight the importance of our approach, specially the role of the Limitedness axiom.
ref: Risk involves two main ideas: loss and variability. In this paper, we combine risk and deviation measures to capture both. Using the proposed Limitedness axiom, we prove that this combination is a coherent, convex, or comonotone risk measure, depending on the properties of its two components. We also give examples of known and new risk measures built within this framework to show the importance of our approach, especially the role of the Limitedness axiom.

source: Common pitfalls in visualization projects include lack of data availability and the domain users' needs and focus changing too rapidly for the design process to complete. While it is often prudent to avoid such projects, we argue it can be beneficial to engage them in some cases as the visualization process can help refine data collection, solving a ` chicken and egg ' problem of having the data and tools to analyze it. We found this to be the case in the domain of task parallel computing . Parallel and distributed programs orchestrate the cooperation of many computation resources to produce results that would be impossible to collect on a single machine.
ref: Visualization projects often fail because data is unavailable or domain users’ needs and priorities change too quickly to finish the design. Although avoiding these projects is often wise, taking them on can sometimes help. The visualization process can improve data collection and break the cycle in which researchers need data to build analysis tools but need those tools to analyze the data. We found this in task-parallel computing. Parallel and distributed programs coordinate many computing resources to produce results that a single machine could not collect.

source: We investigate the problem of dynamic portfolio optimization in continuous-time, finite-horizon setting for a portfolio of two stocks and one risk-free asset. The stocks follow the Cointelation model. The proposed optimization methods are twofold. In what we call an Stochastic Differential Equation approach , we compute the optimal weights using mean-variance criterion and power utility maximization. We show that dynamically switching between these two optimal strategies by introducing a triggering function can further improve the portfolio returns. We contrast this with the machine learning clustering methodology inspired by the band-wise Gaussian mixture model. The first benefit of the machine learning over the Stochastic Differential Equation approach is that we were able to achieve the same results though a simpler channel.
ref: We study dynamic portfolio optimization over a finite period in continuous time for a portfolio with two stocks and one risk-free asset. The stocks follow the Cointelation model. We propose two optimization methods. In the Stochastic Differential Equation approach, we use the mean-variance criterion and power utility maximization to calculate the optimal weights. We show that dynamically switching between these two optimal strategies with a triggering function can further improve portfolio returns. We compare this approach with a machine learning clustering method inspired by the band-wise Gaussian mixture model. The first advantage of machine learning over the Stochastic Differential Equation approach is that it achieved the same results more simply.

source: We attempt to explain stock market dynamics in terms of the interaction among three variables: market price, investor opinion and information flow. We propose a framework for such interaction upon which are based two models of stock market dynamics : the model for empirical study and its extended version for theoretical study . We demonstrate that these models replicate observed stock market behavior on all relevant timescales (from days to years) reasonably well. Using the models , we obtain and discuss a number of results that pose implications for current market theory and offer potential practical applications.
ref: We explain stock market dynamics through the interaction of three variables: market price, investor opinion, and information flow. We propose a framework for this interaction and use it to build two models: one for empirical study and an extended version for theoretical study. We show that these models reproduce observed stock market behavior reasonably well across all relevant timescales, from days to years. We use the models to produce and discuss several results with implications for current market theory and potential practical uses.

source: In this paper, we present a novel method for analysis and segmentation of laminar structure of the cortex based on tissue characteristics whose change across the gray matter facilitates distinction between cortical layers. We develop and analyze features of individual neurons to investigate changes in architectonic differentiation and present a novel high-performance, automated tree-ensemble method trained on data manually labeled by three human investigators. From the location and basic measures of neurons, more complex features are developed and used in machine learning models for automatic segmentation of cortical layers. Tree ensembles are used on data manually labeled by three human experts.
ref: We present a new method for analyzing and segmenting the cortex’s layered structure using tissue characteristics that change across the gray matter and help distinguish cortical layers. We develop and analyze features of individual neurons to study changes in architectonic differentiation. Using neuron locations and basic measurements, we derive more complex features and use them in machine-learning models to segment cortical layers automatically. Our high-performance automated method uses tree ensembles trained on data manually labeled by three human experts.

source: We derive (1) an unbiased estimator for the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio when the in-sample Sharpe ratio is obtained by optimizing over a k-dimensional parameter space . The estimator corrects the in-sample Sharpe ratio for both : noise fit and estimation error. We then show (2) how to use the corrected Sharpe ratio as model selection criterion analogous to the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Selecting a model with the highest corrected Sharpe ratio selects the model with the highest estimated out-of-sample Sharpe ratio in the same way as selection by AIC does for the log-likelihood as measure of fit.
ref: We derive (1) an unbiased estimator of the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio when the in-sample Sharpe ratio comes from optimization over a k-dimensional parameter space. The estimator adjusts the in-sample Sharpe ratio for noise fit and estimation error. We then show (2) how to use the corrected Sharpe ratio as a model-selection criterion similar to the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Choosing the model with the highest corrected Sharpe ratio selects the model with the highest estimated out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, just as AIC selects a model based on log-likelihood as the measure of fit.

source: We present a novel approach to nonparametric identification and consistent estimation in economic models using `proxy controls'. Our approach is particularly well-suited to the context of panel data with a fixed time-dimension but also applies in cross-sectional settings. Proxy controls are proxies for unobserved `perfect controls', where perfect controls are variables that are sufficient for the association between potential outcomes and treatments . Our identification strategy requires that the set of available proxy controls be split into two subsets, one subset acting as an instrument for the other. In the panel case, observations from different periods can be used as proxy controls and our key identifying assumptions follow from restrictions on the serial dependence  of the data .
ref: We present a new way to identify and consistently estimate economic models nonparametrically using “proxy controls.” This approach is especially suited to panel data with a fixed number of time periods, but it also applies to cross-sectional data. Proxy controls stand in for unobserved “perfect controls,” which are variables sufficient to account for the association between potential outcomes and treatments. Our identification strategy requires dividing the available proxy controls into two groups, with one group serving as an instrument for the other. For panel data, observations from different periods can serve as proxy controls, and our main identification assumptions follow from limits on the data’s serial dependence.

source: BACKGROUND : Left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy is a strong predictor of cardiovascular outcomes, but its genetic regulation remains largely unexplained. Conventional phenotyping relies on manual calculation of LV mass and wall thickness, but advanced cardiac image analysis presents an opportunity for high-throughput mapping of genotype-phenotype associations in three dimensions (3D). METHODS : High-resolution cardiac magnetic resonance images were automatically segmented in 1,124 healthy volunteers to create a 3D shape model of the heart. Mass univariate regression was used to plot a 3D effect-size map for the association between wall thickness and a set of predictors at each vertex in the mesh.
ref:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy strongly predicts cardiovascular outcomes, but its genetic regulation remains largely unexplained. Conventional methods require manual calculation of LV mass and wall thickness. Advanced cardiac image analysis could instead map genotype-phenotype associations in three dimensions (3D) at high volume.

METHODS: We automatically segmented high-resolution cardiac magnetic resonance images from 1,124 healthy volunteers to create a 3D model of heart shape. At each vertex in the mesh, we used mass univariate regression to plot a 3D map of the effect size for the association between wall thickness and a set of predictors.

source: We consider rigid spherical particles coated with binding ligands and study their attachment in quiescent flow . This class of fluid-immersed adhesion is widespread in many natural and engineering settings. Our theory highlights how the physics of the binding kinetics of these ligands (expressed through the collision factor function) as well as the attractive / repulsive surface potential in an ionic medium effects the eventual size of these particle aggregates (flocs). As an application of our theory, we consider a microbial population of spherical bacteria. Our results suggest that the elastic ligands allow large floc aggregates by inducing efficient inter-floc collisions (i.e., a large, non-zero collision factor).
ref: We study how rigid spherical particles coated with binding ligands attach in still fluid. This type of adhesion in fluids is common in many natural and engineering settings. Our theory shows how ligand-binding kinetics, expressed through the collision factor function, and attractive or repulsive surface potentials in an ionic medium affect the final size of particle aggregates, or flocs. We apply the theory to a microbial population of spherical bacteria. Our results suggest that elastic ligands enable large flocs by promoting efficient collisions between flocs—that is, a large, nonzero collision factor.

source: We develop a new approach for estimating average treatment effects in the observational studies with unobserved cluster-level heterogeneity. The previous approach relied heavily on linear fixed effect specifications that severely limit the heterogeneity between clusters. These methods imply that linearly adjusting for differences between clusters in average covariate values addresses all concerns with cross-cluster comparisons. Instead, we consider an exponential family structure on the within-cluster distribution of covariates and treatments that implies that a low-dimensional sufficient statistic can summarize the empirical distribution, where this sufficient statistic may include functions of the data beyond average covariate values. Then we use modern causal inference methods to construct flexible and robust estimators .
ref: We develop a new way to estimate average treatment effects in observational studies with unobserved differences between clusters. The previous approach relied heavily on linear fixed-effects models, which severely restrict how clusters can differ. These methods assume that linearly adjusting for differences in clusters’ average covariate values resolves all concerns about comparisons across clusters. Instead, we impose an exponential-family structure on the within-cluster distribution of covariates and treatments. This structure allows a low-dimensional sufficient statistic to summarize the empirical distribution and may include functions of the data beyond average covariate values. We then use modern causal inference methods to build flexible, robust estimators.

source: The problem of computing the exact stretch factor (i.e., the tight bound on the worst case stretch factor) of a Delaunay triangulation has been open for more than three decades . Over the years, a series of upper and lower bounds on the exact stretch factor have been obtained but the gap between them is still large. An alternative approach to solving the problem is to develop techniques for computing the exact stretch factor of "easier" types of Delaunay triangulations, in particular those defined using regular-polygons instead of a circle. Tight bounds exist for Delaunay triangulations defined using an equilateral triangle and a square.
ref: Computing the exact stretch factor of a Delaunay triangulation—that is, the tight bound on its worst-case stretch factor—has remained an open problem for more than three decades. Researchers have found several upper and lower bounds, but a large gap remains between them. Another approach is to develop methods for computing the exact stretch factor of simpler types of Delaunay triangulations, especially those defined by regular polygons rather than a circle. Tight bounds are known for Delaunay triangulations defined by an equilateral triangle or a square.

source: We determine the optimal strategy for investing in a Black-Scholes market in order to maximize the probability that wealth at death meets a bequest goal b . We, thereby, make more objective the goal of maximizing expected utility of death, first considered in a continuous-time framework by Merton (1969). Specifically, instead of requiring the individual tochoose a utility function, we only require the individual to choose a bequest goal b. We learn that, for wealth lying between 0 and b , the optimal investment strategy is {\it independent } of b , a surprising result. Therefore, if the individual were to revise her bequest goal, her investment strategy would not change if her wealth is less than the new goal .
ref: We find the best investment strategy in a Black-Scholes market for maximizing the probability that wealth at death reaches a bequest goal, b. This makes Merton’s (1969) continuous-time goal of maximizing expected utility at death more objective. Instead of asking the individual to choose a utility function, we ask her only to choose a bequest goal, b. Surprisingly, when wealth is between 0 and b, the best investment strategy does not depend on b. Thus, if the individual changes her bequest goal, her investment strategy will stay the same as long as her wealth is below the new goal.

source: The man who took a gut feel of seeing personal computers in every household three decades and each will require a stable operating system will now pursue philanthropic activities under the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. As Gates leaves day-to-day operations, two people will assume the his two vital duties. Craig Mundie will handle the company's long-term planning while Ray Ozzie will handle the operations. Bill Gates founded Microsoft in 1975 and from then has dominated the market for operating systems in personal computers. Gates managed close to 78,000 employees in 103 countries all over the world.
ref: Three decades ago, Bill Gates envisioned a personal computer in every home, each needing a stable operating system. He will now focus on philanthropy through the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. As Gates steps away from day-to-day operations, two people will take over his key duties. Craig Mundie will lead the company’s long-term planning, while Ray Ozzie will run operations. Gates founded Microsoft in 1975 and has since dominated the personal computer operating system market. He managed nearly 78,000 employees in 103 countries.

source: On 2018-01-17 two electron crystallography structures (with PDB entries 6AXZ, 6BTK) on a prion protofibril of bank vole PrP(168-176) (a segment in the PrP \beta2-\alpha2 loop) were released into the PDB Bank. The paper published by [Nat Struct Mol Biol 25(2):131-134 (2018)] reports some polar clasps for these two crystal structures, and "an intersheet hydrogen bond between Tyr169 and the backbone carbonyl of Asn171 on an opposing strand." However , by revisiting the polar clasps, we cannot confirm this very important intersheet hydrogen bond; instead we found another hydrogen bond ( Asn171 :H-Gln172: OE1  between the strand  of one sheet and the opposing strand  of the mating sheet ) to replace it .
ref: On 2018-01-17, two electron crystallography structures of a bank vole PrP(168–176) prion protofibril, a segment in the PrP β2–α2 loop, were released in the PDB Bank as entries 6AXZ and 6BTK. The paper in Nat Struct Mol Biol 25(2):131–134 (2018) reports several polar clasps in these crystal structures and “an intersheet hydrogen bond between Tyr169 and the backbone carbonyl of Asn171 on an opposing strand.” However, when we revisited the polar clasps, we could not confirm this important intersheet hydrogen bond. Instead, we found another hydrogen bond, Asn171:H–Gln172:OE1, between a strand in one sheet and the opposing strand in the mating sheet, which replaces it.

source: This article develops a new risk management framework for companies on the basis of the leverage process (a ratio of company asset value over its debt). We approach this task by time reversal, last passage time, and the h-transform of linear diffusions. For general diffusions with killing, we obtain the probability density of the last passage time to a certain alarming level and analyze the distribution of the time left until killing after the last passage time to that level. We then apply these results to the leverage process of the company. Finally, we suggest how a company should determine the aforementioned alarming level . Specifically, we construct a relevant optimization problem and derive an optimal alarming level as its solution .
ref: This article develops a new risk management framework for companies based on the leverage process, defined as the ratio of a company’s asset value to its debt. We use time reversal, last passage time, and the h-transform of linear diffusions. For general diffusions with killing, we find the probability density of the last passage time to a given alarming level and analyze the distribution of the time remaining until killing after that last passage. We then apply these results to a company’s leverage process. Finally, we propose a way for a company to set the alarming level by formulating an optimization problem and deriving the optimal level from its solution.

source: While large-scale contextual language models have enjoyed great success recently, much remains to be understood about what is encoded in their representations. In this work, we characterize how contextual representations of concrete nouns extracted by trained language models relate to the physical properties of the objects they refer to. Our approach uses a probing model that examines how effective these language representations are in discerning between different visual representations. We show that many recent language models yield representations that are useful in retrieving semantically aligned image patches , and explore the role of context in this process. Much weaker results are found in control experiments, attesting the selectivity of the probe.
ref: Large contextual language models have succeeded in recent years, but we still do not fully understand what their representations encode. We study how trained language models represent concrete nouns and how those representations relate to the physical properties of the objects the nouns refer to. We use a probing model to test how well these language representations distinguish among visual representations. We show that representations from many recent language models can retrieve semantically matching image patches, and we examine how context affects this process. Control experiments produce much weaker results, showing that the probe is selective.

source: Banks must manage the lifetime costs of XVA, i. e. credit (CVA), funding(including funding of initial margins, FVA and MVA), capital (KVA) and tax(TVA). Management includes hedging(requiring first- and second-order sensitivities), attribution (and re-attribution), and incremental changes together with their interactions. Incremental management is required throughout the trading day for multiple portfolio changes. We show that a combination of trade-level regression and global conditioning (exploiting the linearity of conditional expectations over filtrations) radically simplifies both the computation and also the implementation of the computations . Moreover, many calculation elements are inherently parallel and suitable for GPU implementation  .
ref: Banks must manage XVA costs over their lifetime: credit (CVA), funding—including funding initial margins (FVA and MVA)—capital (KVA), and tax (TVA). This includes hedging, which requires first- and second-order sensitivities; attribution and re-attribution; and incremental changes and their interactions. Banks must manage these incremental effects throughout the trading day as portfolios change multiple times. We show that combining trade-level regression with global conditioning, using the linearity of conditional expectations over filtrations, greatly simplifies the calculations and their implementation. Many parts of the calculation are also inherently parallel and well suited to GPUs.

source: We consider a model of optimal investment and consumption with both habit formation and partial observations in incomplete It\^{o} processes markets. The individual investor develops addictive consumption habits gradually while only observing the market stock prices but not the instantaneous rate of return , which follows an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process . Applying the Kalman-Bucy filtering theorem and  Dynamic Programming arguments, we solve the associated HJB equation explicitly for this path dependent stochastic control problem in the case of power utility preferences . We provide the optimal investment and consumption policies in explicit feedback forms using rigorous verification arguments.
ref: We study optimal investment and consumption with habit formation and partial observation in incomplete markets governed by Itô processes. The individual investor gradually develops addictive consumption habits and observes only stock prices, not the instantaneous rate of return, which follows an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Using the Kalman–Bucy filtering theorem and dynamic programming, we explicitly solve the associated HJB equation for this path-dependent stochastic control problem when the investor has power utility preferences. Through rigorous verification, we give the optimal investment and consumption policies in explicit feedback form.

source: We have experimentally investigated the transitions of collective motions of bacterial cells in a shallow circular pool using the bacterial species Bacillus subtilis. In our previous paper, we reported that the collective motions were classified into the six phases on a phase diagram with the two parameters,  the reduced cell length \lambda \ and the cell density \rho. In the present study, we focused on the sharp transitions at \lambda\cong0.1 (\equiv \rm C1) with low values of \rho between the random motion phase and the one-way rotational motion phase. By introducing the order parameter Q which measures the aligned cell motion along the circumferential direction of a pool, the transitions at \lambda=\rm C1 were clearly characterized. Based on the detailed observations of single-cell trajectories in a pool, we verified that the effect of cell-noise interactions was widely distributed. We conclude that, even in such random environment,  sharp transitions of collective motions were caused by the cell-cell interactions at \lambda=\rm C1.
ref: We experimentally studied changes in the collective motion of Bacillus subtilis cells in a shallow circular pool. In our previous paper, we classified these motions into six phases on a phase diagram based on two parameters: reduced cell length \(\lambda\) and cell density \(\rho\). In this study, we focused on the sharp transitions at \(\lambda \cong 0.1\) (\(\equiv \mathrm{C1}\)) and low \(\rho\), between the random-motion phase and the one-way rotational-motion phase. We clearly characterized the transitions at \(\lambda=\mathrm{C1}\) using an order parameter, \(Q\), that measures how closely cell motion aligns with the pool’s circumference. Detailed observations of individual cell paths in the pool confirmed that the effects of cell-noise interactions were widely distributed. We conclude that, even in this random environment, cell-cell interactions caused sharp transitions in collective motion at \(\lambda=\mathrm{C1}\).

source: Our in silico model was built to investigate the development process of the adaptive immune system. For simplicity, we concentrated on humoral immunity and its major components: T cells, B cells, antibodies, interleukins, non-immune self cells, and foreign antigens. Our model is a microscopic one, similar to the interacting particle models of statistical physics . Events are considered random and modelled by a continuous time, finite state Markov process, that is, they are controlled by  independent exponential clocks. Our main purpose was to compare different theoretical models of the adaptive immune system and self--nonself discrimination: the ones that are described by well-known textbooks, and a novel one developed by our research group. Our theoretical model emphasizes the hypothesis that the immune system of a fetus can primarily learn what self is but unable to prepare itself for the huge, unknown variety of nonself. The simulation begins after conception, by developing the immune system from scratch and learning the set of self antigens. The simulation ends several months after births when a more-or-less stationary state of the immune system has been established.
ref: We built our computer model to study how the adaptive immune system develops. For simplicity, we focused on humoral immunity and its main components: T cells, B cells, antibodies, interleukins, non-immune self cells, and foreign antigens. The model works at the microscopic level and resembles the interacting-particle models used in statistical physics. It treats events as random and models them as a continuous-time, finite-state Markov process controlled by independent exponential clocks. Our main goal was to compare different theories of the adaptive immune system and how it distinguishes self from nonself. These included theories described in well-known textbooks and a new theory developed by our research group. Our theory emphasizes the hypothesis that a fetus’s immune system can mainly learn what is self but cannot prepare for the vast, unknown variety of nonself. The simulation starts after conception, develops the immune system from scratch, and learns the set of self antigens. It ends several months after birth, when the immune system has reached a more or less stable state.

source: This paper explains predictions of image captioning models with attention mechanisms beyond visualizing the attention itself. In this paper, we develop variants of layer-wise relevance backpropagation (LRP) and gradient backpropagation , tailored to image captioning models with attention mechanisms. The explanations provide simultaneously pixel-wise image explanation and linguistic explanation for each word in the captions. We show that given a word in the caption to be explained, explanation methods such as LRP reveal supporting and opposing pixels as well as preceding words. We compare the properties of attention heatmaps systematically against those computed with explanation methods such as LRP, Grad-CAM  and Guided Grad-CAM. We show that explanation methods , firstly, correlate to object locations with higher precisionthan attention, secondly, are able to identify object wordsthat are unsupported by image content, and thirdly, provide guidance to improve and de-bias the model. Results are reported using two different image captioning attention models trained with Flickr30K and MSCOCO2017 datasets. Experimental analyses show the strength of explanation methods for understanding image captioning attention models .
ref: This paper explains the predictions of attention-based image captioning models, going beyond attention visualizations. We develop versions of layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and gradient backpropagation tailored to these models. For each word in a caption, the methods explain both the relevant image pixels and the linguistic context. Given a caption word, methods such as LRP identify supporting and opposing pixels and preceding words. We systematically compare attention heatmaps with explanations produced by LRP, Grad-CAM, and Guided Grad-CAM. We show that these explanation methods locate objects more precisely than attention, identify object words unsupported by the image, and help improve and reduce bias in the model. We report results for two attention-based image captioning models trained on the Flickr30K and MSCOCO2017 datasets. Our experiments show that explanation methods help us understand attention-based image captioning models.

source: In nonlinear time series analysis and dynamical systems theory, Takens' embedding theorem states that the sliding window embedding of a generic observation along finite, uniformly sampled trajectories in a state space, recovers a sampling of the region traversed by the dynamics. This can be used, for instance, to show that sliding window embeddings of periodic signals recover topological loops, and that sliding window embeddings of quasiperiodic signals recover high-dimensional torii. However, in spite of these motivating examples, Takens' theorem does not in general prescribe how to choose such an observation function given particular dynamics in a state space. In this work, we state conditions on observation functions defined on compact Riemannian manifolds, that lead to successful reconstructions for particular dynamics. We apply our theory and construct families of time series whose sliding window embeddings trace tori, Klein bottles, spheres, and projective planes. This greatly enriches the set of examples of time series known to concentrate on various shapes via sliding window embeddings  . We also present numerical experiments showing that we can recover low dimensional representations of the underlying dynamics on state space, by using the persistent cohomology of sliding window embeddings and Eilenberg-MacLane (i.e., circular and real projective) coordinates.
ref: In nonlinear time series analysis and dynamical systems theory, Takens’ embedding theorem says that a sliding window embedding of a generic observation along finite, uniformly sampled trajectories in a state space recovers a sample of the region the dynamics traverse. For example, sliding window embeddings of periodic signals recover topological loops, while those of quasiperiodic signals recover high-dimensional tori. Despite these examples, Takens’ theorem does not generally explain how to choose an observation function for specific dynamics in a state space. Here, we give conditions for observation functions on compact Riemannian manifolds that produce successful reconstructions for particular dynamics. We apply this theory to build families of time series whose sliding window embeddings trace tori, Klein bottles, spheres, and projective planes. This greatly expands the known examples of time series whose sliding window embeddings concentrate on different shapes. We also present numerical experiments showing that persistent cohomology of sliding window embeddings and Eilenberg–MacLane coordinates—that is, circular and real projective coordinates—can recover low-dimensional representations of the underlying dynamics on the state space.

source: This paper provides a testing approach for detecting sample selection in nonparametric conditional quantile functions. Our testing strategy consists of a two-step procedure: the first test is an omitted predictor test with the propensity score as the omitted variable. As with any omnibus test, in the case of rejection we cannot distinguish between rejection due to genuine selection or to misspecification. Thus, since the differentiation of the two causes has implications for nonparametric (point) identification and estimation of the conditional quantile function(s), we suggest a second test to identify whether the cause for rejection at the first stage was solely due to selection or not. Using only individuals with propensity score close to one, this second test relies on an `identification at infinity' argument, but accommodates cases of irregular identification. Our testing procedure does not require any parametric assumptions on the selection equation , and all our results hold uniformly across quantile ranks in a compact set. We apply our procedure to test for selection in log hourly wages using UK Family Expenditure Survey data  .
ref: This paper presents a way to test for sample selection in nonparametric conditional quantile functions. The method has two steps. First, we run an omitted-predictor test that treats the propensity score as the omitted variable. Like any omnibus test, a rejection cannot show whether genuine selection or misspecification caused it. Because distinguishing these causes affects the nonparametric point identification and estimation of the conditional quantile function or functions, we propose a second test. This test determines whether selection alone caused the first-stage rejection. It uses only individuals with propensity scores close to one and draws on an “identification at infinity” argument, while allowing for irregular identification. The procedure makes no parametric assumptions about the selection equation, and all results hold uniformly across quantile ranks in a compact set. We apply the procedure to UK Family Expenditure Survey data to test for selection in log hourly wages.

source: Backpropagation is driving today's artificial neural networks (ANNs). However, despite extensive research, it remains unclear if the brain implements this algorithm. Among neuroscientists, reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are often seen as a realistic alternative: neurons can randomly introduce change, and use unspecific feedback signals to observe their effect on the cost and thus approximate their gradient. However, the convergence rate of such learning scales poorly with the number of involved neurons (e. g. O(N)). Here we propose a hybrid learning approach. Each neuron uses an RL-type strategy to learn how to approximate the gradients that backpropagation would provide -- in this way it learns to learn . We provide proof that our approach converges to the true gradient for certain classes of networks. In both feed-forward and recurrent networks, we empirically show that our approach learns to approximate the gradient, and can match the performance of gradient-based learning. Learning to learn provides a biologically plausible mechanism of achieving good performance, without the need for precise, pre-specified learning rules.
ref: Backpropagation powers today’s artificial neural networks (ANNs). But despite extensive research, we still do not know whether the brain uses this algorithm. Neuroscientists often see reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms as a realistic alternative: neurons can introduce random changes and use nonspecific feedback signals to measure how those changes affect the cost, allowing them to approximate the gradient. However, the convergence rate of this kind of learning scales poorly with the number of neurons involved—for example, O(N). We propose a hybrid approach. Each neuron uses an RL-type strategy to learn to approximate the gradients that backpropagation would provide. In this way, it learns to learn. We prove that our approach converges to the true gradient for certain classes of networks. In experiments with both feed-forward and recurrent networks, our approach learns to approximate the gradient and can match the performance of gradient-based learning. Learning to learn offers a biologically plausible way to achieve good performance without precise, pre-specified learning rules.

source: In an arbitrage-free financial market, asset prices (including dividends) should not exhibit jumps of a predictable magnitude at predictable times. We provide a rigorous formulation of this result in a fully general setting, without imposing any semimartingale restriction and only allowing for buy-and-hold positions. We prove that asset prices do not exhibit predictable jumps if and only if there is no possibility of obtaining sure profits via high-frequency limits of buy-and-hold trading strategies . We furthermore show that right-continuity is an indispensable requirement for any price process that does not admit sure profits. Our results are robust with respect to  transaction costs or model mis-specifications and imply that, under minimal assumptions, price changes occurring at scheduled dates should only be due to unanticipated information releases.
ref: In an arbitrage-free financial market, asset prices, including dividends, should not jump by predictable amounts at predictable times. We state this result rigorously in a fully general setting, without requiring semimartingales and using only buy-and-hold positions. We prove that asset prices have no predictable jumps if and only if traders cannot earn sure profits through high-frequency limits of buy-and-hold strategies. We also show that any price process that does not allow sure profits must be right-continuous. Our results hold despite transaction costs or model errors and imply that, under minimal assumptions, price changes on scheduled dates should result only from unexpected information releases.

source: Circadian rhythms are acquired through evolution to increase the chances for survival by synchronizing to the daylight cycle. Reliable synchronization is realized through two trade-off properties: regularity to keep time precisely, and entrainability to synchronize the internal time with daylight. Since both properties have been tuned through natural selection, their adaptation can be formalized in the framework of mathematical optimization. By using a succinct model , we found that simultaneous optimization of regularity and entrainability entails  inherent features of the circadian mechanism irrespective of model details . At the behavioral level we discovered the existence of a dead zone, a time during which light pulses neither advance nor delay the clock. At the molecular level we demonstrate the role-sharing of two light inputs, phase advance and delay, as is well observed in mammals. We also reproduce the results of phase-controlling experiments and predict molecular elements responsible for the clockwork . Our results indicate that circadian clocks function optimally and that a simple mathematical model can illuminate many complex phenomena observed in nature .
ref: Circadian rhythms evolved to improve survival by syncing with the daylight cycle. Reliable synchronization depends on a trade-off between two properties: regularity, which keeps time precisely, and entrainability, which aligns internal time with daylight. Because natural selection has tuned both properties, their adaptation can be expressed as a mathematical optimization problem. Using a concise model, we found that optimizing regularity and entrainability at the same time produces features inherent to circadian mechanisms, regardless of the model’s details. At the behavioral level, we found a dead zone: a period when light pulses neither advance nor delay the clock. At the molecular level, we show how two light inputs divide the roles of advancing and delaying the clock, as commonly observed in mammals. We also reproduce the results of phase-control experiments and predict which molecular elements drive the clockwork. Our results suggest that circadian clocks work optimally and that a simple mathematical model can explain many complex phenomena observed in nature.

source: Discovering new intents is a crucial task in a dialogue system . Most existing methods are limited in transferring the prior knowledge from known intents to new intents. These methods also have difficulties in providing high-quality supervised signals to learn clustering-friendly features for grouping unlabeled intents. In this work, we propose an effective method (Deep Aligned Clustering) to discover new intents with the aid of limited known intent data. Firstly, we leverage a few labeled known intent samples as prior knowledge to pre-train the model. Then, we perform k-means to produce cluster assignments as pseudo-labels. Moreover, we propose an alignment strategy to tackle the label inconsistency  during clustering assignments. Finally, we learn the intent representations under the supervision of the aligned pseudo-labels. With an unknown number of new intents, we predict the number of intent categories by eliminating low-confidence intent-wise clusters. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that our method is more robust and achieves substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art methods.( Code available at URL
ref: Discovering new intents is essential for dialogue systems. Most existing methods struggle to transfer prior knowledge from known intents to new ones. They also struggle to provide high-quality supervision for learning features that help group unlabeled intents. We propose an effective method, Deep Aligned Clustering, that uses limited data from known intents to discover new ones. First, we use a few labeled examples of known intents as prior knowledge to pretrain the model. We then use k-means to assign clusters as pseudo-labels. We also use an alignment strategy to resolve inconsistent labels across clustering assignments. Finally, we learn intent representations using the aligned pseudo-labels as supervision. When the number of new intents is unknown, we estimate the number of intent categories by removing low-confidence intent-wise clusters. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that our method is more robust and substantially improves on state-of-the-art methods. (Code available at URL

ref: This change in stability is closely linked to the network’s connectance. Evidence also points to a sharp shift in the network’s structure in the 1960s and 1970s, when most measures of robustness rose quickly before starting to decline again.
