Scientists often cite poor intuition as a challenge, especially when interpreting research on probability and statistics. One popular way to build statistical intuition is to imagine a game of chance with clear financial outcomes. In 1956, Kelly used this method to give an intuitive interpretation of relative entropy.¹ He studied an investor who seeks to maximize growth in a game with mutually exclusive outcomes—a “horse race.” He showed that the investor’s expected rate of return equals the relative entropy that measures the difference between the investor’s probability estimates and the official odds. In effect, Kelly showed that, on average, a growth-maximizing investor would expect to turn 1 bit of extra information into a 100% return on investment. Despite the mathematics, Samuelson strongly criticized this interpretation as dangerous because most people do not seek to maximize growth.²˒³

Here we show that a deeper link between information and expected returns is indeed real. Compared with the Kelly information benchmark, differences in people’s risk aversion do reduce expected returns. But information also determines the size of that reduction: it is proportional to the absolute difference between relative entropy and its celebrated generalization, the Rényi divergence.⁴ Because scientists and engineers widely use the Rényi divergence, and because financial returns are much easier to imagine, we expect this intuition to be useful across many fields.

source: How stable and general is behavior once reached maximum learning ? To answer this question and understand post-acquisition behavior and its related individual differences, we propose a psychological principle that naturally extends the basic associative single-cue Rescorla-Wagner model (which may also be called Hull model) of Pavlovian conditioning to (i) a framework of dynamical models predicting resistance to learning in the first few sessions followed by an over-optimal response peak . In turn, (ii) the theory can be further extended to describe response fluctuations by the laws of quantum mechanics. (iii) We also introduce an independent model characterized by the presence of a stochastic noise of cognitive origin . We ran an unusually long experiment with 32 rats over 3960 trials, where we excluded habituation and other well-known phenomena as sources of variability in the subjects' performance. There is weak to positive evidence that Hull model is the best nonlinear regression to averaged data only for a minority of the subjects, while its dynamical extension (i) can explain the  totality of data . The noise encountered in all individual responses is white , thus confirming the simplest version of model (iii) but standing in contrast with the colored-noise findings in human performance . Finally, data are compatible with the quantum extension (ii), although experimental uncertainties dominate the result. On the other hand, data do not favor models with (iv) a long-memory effect or (v) where response variability is solely described by a random fractal .
ref:
How stable and general is behavior once maximum learning has been reached? To answer this question and understand behavior after acquisition and the related differences between individuals, we propose a psychological principle that extends the basic associative, single-cue Rescorla-Wagner model of Pavlovian conditioning, also called the Hull model. This principle extends the model to (i) a set of dynamic models that predict resistance to learning during the first few sessions, followed by a response peak above the optimal level. The theory can then be extended further to (ii) describe response fluctuations using the laws of quantum mechanics. We also introduce (iii) an independent model that includes random noise of cognitive origin.

We ran an unusually long experiment with 32 rats over 3,960 trials. We ruled out habituation and other well-known phenomena as sources of variation in the subjects’ performance. There is weak to positive evidence that the Hull model provides the best nonlinear fit to averaged data for only a minority of the subjects, while its dynamic extension (i) can explain all the data. The noise in every individual response is white, which confirms the simplest version of model (iii) but contrasts with findings of colored noise in human performance. Finally, the data are compatible with the quantum extension (ii), although experimental uncertainty dominates the result. However, the data do not favor models that include (iv) a long-memory effect or (v) describe response variation solely as a random fractal.

source: Bacteria communicate using external chemical signals called autoinducers (AI) in a process known as quorum sensing (QS). QS efficiency is reduced by both limitations of AI diffusion and potential interference from neighboring strains. There is thus a need for theoretical approaches that yield nontrivial quantitative predictions of how spatial community structure shapes information processing in complex microbial ecosystems. As a step in this direction, we apply a reaction-diffusion model to study autoinducer signaling dynamics in a growing bacterial community as a function of the density of metapopulations, or spatially dispersed colonies , in the total system. We predict a non-equilibrium phase transition between a local quorum sensing (LQS) regime at low dispersal, with AI signaling dynamics primarily controlled by the local population density of colonies, and a global quorum sensing (GQS) regime at high dispersal , with the dynamics being governed by the collective metapopulation density. In addition, we propose an observable order parameter for this system, termed the Neighbor Interference Fraction (NIF), which accounts for the ratio of neighbor-produced to self-produced signal at a colony. The transition between LQS to GQS is intimately connected to a tradeoff between the signaling network's latency, or speed of activation, and its throughput, or the total spatial range over which all the components of the system communicate . Levels of dispersal near the phase boundary provide an optimal compromise that enables simultaneously high latency and throughput in a given environment .
ref: Bacteria communicate through external chemical signals called autoinducers (AI), a process known as quorum sensing (QS). Limited AI diffusion and possible interference from neighboring strains reduce the efficiency of QS. We therefore need theoretical methods that make nontrivial, quantitative predictions about how a community’s spatial structure shapes information processing in complex microbial ecosystems. As a step toward this goal, we use a reaction-diffusion model to study autoinducer signaling in a growing bacterial community at different densities of metapopulations—spatially dispersed colonies—across the whole system. We predict a non-equilibrium phase transition between two regimes. At low dispersal, local quorum sensing (LQS) dominates, and the local population density of colonies primarily controls AI signaling. At high dispersal, global quorum sensing (GQS) dominates, and the collective metapopulation density controls signaling. We also propose an observable order parameter called the Neighbor Interference Fraction (NIF), which measures the ratio of signals produced by neighboring colonies to signals produced by the colony itself. The shift from LQS to GQS is closely tied to a tradeoff between the signaling network’s latency, or activation speed, and its throughput, or the total spatial range across which all parts of the system communicate. Dispersal levels near the phase boundary offer an optimal balance that allows both high latency and high throughput in a given environment.

source: Patients increasingly turn to search engines and online content before, or in place of, talking with a health professional. Low quality health information, which is common on the internet, presents risks to the patient in the form of misinformation and a possibly poorer relationship to their physician. To address this, the DISCERN criteria (developed at University of Oxford) are used to evaluate the quality of online health information. However, patients are unlikely to take the time to apply these criteria to the health websites they visit. We built an automated implementation of the DISCERN instrument (Brief version) using machine learning models. We compared the use of a traditional model (Random Forest) with  a hierarchical encoder attention-based neural network (HEA) model using two language embeddings based on BERT and BioBERT. The HEA BERT and BioBERT models achieved  F1-macro scores averaging 0.75 and 0.74, respectively, on all criteria outperforming the Random Forest model (  F1-macro = 0.69). Similarly,  HEA BERT and BioBERT scored on average 0.8 and 0.81 (F1-micro) vs. 0.76 for the Random Forest model. Overall, the neural network based models achieved 81\% and 86\% average accuracy at 100\% and 80\% coverage, respectively, compared to 94\% manual rating accuracy. The attention mechanism implemented in the HEA architectures provided 'model explainability' by identifying reasonable supporting sentences for the documents fulfilling the Brief DISCERN criteria. Our research suggests that it is feasible to automate online health information quality assessment, which is an important step towards empowering patients to become informed partners in the healthcare process.
ref:
Patients increasingly use search engines and online content before talking with a health professional, or instead of doing so. Low-quality health information is common online and can expose patients to misinformation and possibly harm their relationship with their physician. The DISCERN criteria, developed at the University of Oxford, assess the quality of online health information. However, patients are unlikely to spend time applying these criteria to the health websites they visit.

We used machine learning to automate the Brief DISCERN instrument. We compared a traditional Random Forest model with a hierarchical encoder attention-based neural network (HEA) using language embeddings based on BERT and BioBERT. Across all criteria, the HEA BERT and BioBERT models achieved average F1-macro scores of 0.75 and 0.74, respectively, outperforming the Random Forest model, which scored 0.69. The HEA BERT and BioBERT models also achieved average F1-micro scores of 0.80 and 0.81, compared with 0.76 for the Random Forest model.

Overall, the neural network models achieved average accuracy of 81% at 100% coverage and 86% at 80% coverage, compared with 94% accuracy for manual ratings. The attention mechanism in the HEA architectures made the models explainable by identifying reasonable supporting sentences in documents that met the Brief DISCERN criteria. Our research suggests that automated assessment of online health information quality is feasible. This is an important step toward helping patients become informed partners in healthcare.

source: Given the recent controversies in some neuroimaging statistical methods, we compared the most frequently used functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) analysis packages: AFNI, FSL and SPM, with regard to temporal autocorrelation modeling. We used both resting state and task-based fMRI data, altogether ten datasets containing 780 scans corresponding to different scanning sequences and subject populations. In analyses of each fMRI scan we considered different assumed experimental designs and smoothing levels. For data with no expected experimentally-induced activation, FSL and SPM resulted in much higher false positive rates than AFNI. We showed it was because of residual positive autocorrelation left after pre-whitening. On the other hand, due to SPM modeling temporal autocorrelation in the least flexible way, it can introduce negative autocorrelations during pre-whitening for scans with long repetition times. As a result, for one task-based dataset we observed a large loss of sensitivity when SPM was used. Interestingly, because pre-whitening in FSL and SPM does not remove a substantial part of the temporal autocorrelation in the noise, we found a strong relationship in which the lower the assumed experimental design frequency, the more likely it was to observe significant activation. Though temporal autocorrelation modeling in AFNI was not perfect, its performance was much higher than the performance of temporal autocorrelation modeling in FSL and SPM.  FSL and SPM could improve their autocorrelation modeling approaches for example by adopting a noise modelsimilar to the one used by AFNI .

Recent controversies have raised questions about some neuroimaging statistical methods. We compared how the three most widely used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) analysis packages—AFNI, FSL, and SPM—model temporal autocorrelation. We used resting-state and task-based fMRI data from ten datasets, totaling 780 scans from different scanning sequences and subject populations. For each scan, we tested different assumed experimental designs and smoothing levels.

For data with no expected experimentally induced activation, FSL and SPM produced much higher false-positive rates than AFNI. We showed that this happened because pre-whitening left residual positive autocorrelation. By contrast, because SPM models temporal autocorrelation in the least flexible way, pre-whitening can introduce negative autocorrelation in scans with long repetition times. As a result, we observed a large loss of sensitivity with SPM in one task-based dataset.

Because pre-whitening in FSL and SPM does not remove a substantial part of the noise’s temporal autocorrelation, we also found a strong relationship: the lower the assumed experimental design frequency, the more likely we were to observe significant activation. Although AFNI’s temporal autocorrelation modeling was not perfect, it performed much better than that of FSL and SPM. FSL and SPM could improve their approaches to autocorrelation modeling, for example, by adopting a noise model similar to AFNI’s.

source: Data-driven spatial filtering approaches are commonly used to assess rhythmic brain activity from multichannel recordings such as electroencephalography (EEG). As spatial filter estimationis prone to noise, non-stationarity effects and limited data, a high model variability induced by slight changes of, e.g., involved hyperparametersis generally encountered. These aspects challenge the assessment of functionally relevant features which are of special importance in closed-loop applications as ,  e.g., in the field of rehabilitation. We propose a data-driven method to identify groups of reliable and functionally relevant oscillatory components computed by a spatial filtering approach. Therefore, we initially embrace the variability of decoding models in a large configuration space before condensing information by density-based clustering of components' functional signatures. Exemplified for a hand force task with  rich within-trial structure , the approach was evaluated on EEG data of 18 healthy subjects . We found that functional characteristics of single componentsare revealed by distinct temporal dynamics of their event-related power changes. Based on a within-subject analysis, our clustering revealed seven groups of homogeneous envelope dynamics on average. To support introspection by practitioners, we provide a set of metrics to characterize and validate single clusterings. We show that identified clusters contain components of strictly confined frequency ranges, dominated by the alpha and beta band. Our method is applicable to any spatial filtering algorithm . Despite high model variability, it allows capturing and monitoring relevant oscillatory features . We foresee its application in closed-loop applications such as brain-computer interface based protocols in stroke rehabilitation.

Researchers commonly use data-driven spatial filters to assess rhythmic brain activity in multichannel recordings such as electroencephalography (EEG). Because noise, non-stationarity, and limited data can affect spatial filter estimates, small changes in factors such as hyperparameters often produce large variations among models. This variability makes it harder to assess functionally relevant features, which are especially important in closed-loop applications such as rehabilitation.

We propose a data-driven method for identifying groups of reliable, functionally relevant oscillatory components computed with a spatial filtering method. We first allow decoding models to vary across a large configuration space, then condense the information by using density-based clustering on the components’ functional signatures. We evaluated the method on EEG data from 18 healthy participants performing a hand-force task with rich within-trial structure.

We found that distinct changes over time in event-related power reveal the functional characteristics of individual components. In within-subject analyses, our clustering found an average of seven groups with similar envelope dynamics. To help practitioners examine the results, we provide metrics for characterizing and validating individual clusterings. We show that the identified clusters contain components within strictly limited frequency ranges, mainly in the alpha and beta bands.

Our method works with any spatial filtering algorithm. Despite high model variability, it can capture and monitor relevant oscillatory features. We expect it to be used in closed-loop applications such as brain-computer-interface-based protocols for stroke rehabilitation.

Network models are widely seen as the best way to model complex systems such as epidemics and neuronal activity in the brain. However, in most cases, the exact network on which these processes occur is unknown. This has prompted much research on network inference. Most studies infer network structure from detailed time-series data for individual nodes. Here, we address the harder task of inferring the underlying network family using only population-level incidence data over time.

A major obstacle is the extremely high number of dimensions in the resulting stochastic epidemic model. We address this by approximating the susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) network model with a birth-death process whose rates capture the underlying network structure and disease dynamics. Using systematic simulations, we propose a simple, three-parameter model of these rates and show that different well-known network families occupy distinct regions of its parameter space. This provides a way to characterize different network families in advance.

Given population-level epidemic data over time, we then use a Bayesian classifier to calculate posterior distributions over different network families. Tests on synthetic and real-world networks show that the method produces excellent results. The framework can readily accommodate many network families and spreading processes and could provide a new benchmark for inferring networks from population-level data.

source: In this paper, we study the out-of-sample properties of robust empirical optimization and develop a theory for data-driven calibration of the robustness parameter for worst-case maximization problems with concave reward functions . Building on the intuition that robust optimization reduces the sensitivity of the expected reward to errors in the model by controlling the spread of the reward distribution, we show that the first-order benefit of  little bit of robustness  is a significant reduction in the variance of the out-of-sample reward while the corresponding impact on the mean is almost an order of magnitude smaller. One implication is that a substantial reduction in the variance of the out-of-sample reward (i.e. sensitivityof the expected reward to model misspecification) is possible at little cost if the robustness parameter is properly calibrated. To this end, we introduce the notion of a robust mean-variance frontier to select the robustness parameter and show that it can be approximated using resampling methods like the bootstrap. Robust optimization reduces the sensitivity of expected rewards to model errors by controlling the spread of the reward distribution. This means that a properly calibrated robustness parameter can substantially reduce the variance of out-of-sample rewards—and thus the sensitivity of expected rewards to model misspecification—at little cost. We introduce a robust mean-variance frontier for selecting the robustness parameter and show that resampling methods such as the bootstrap can approximate it. Our examples also show that open-loop calibration methods, such as choosing a 90% confidence level regardless of the data and objective function, can produce solutions that are very conservative out of sample. By contrast, choosing the robustness parameter to optimize an estimate of the expected out-of-sample reward, such as through the bootstrap, without considering variance often produces solutions that are not robust enough.

source: In the (1+\varepsilon,r) -approximate-near-neighbor problem for curves (ANNC) under some distance measure \delta, the goal is to construct a data structure for a given set C of curves that supports approximate near-neighbor queries: Given a query curve Q, if there exists a curve C\inC such that \delta(Q,C)\le r, then return a curve C'\inC with \delta(Q,C')\le(1+\varepsilon)r. There exists an efficient reduction from the (1+\varepsilon) -approximate-nearest-neighbor problem to ANNC, where in the former problem the answer to a query is a curve C\inC with \delta(Q,C)\le(1+\varepsilon)\cdot\delta(Q,C^*), where C^* is the curve of C closest to Q. Given a set C of n curves, each consisting of m points in d dimensions, we construct a data structure for ANNC that uses n\cdot O(1{\varepsilon})^{md} storage space and has O(md \log(\frac{nm{\varepsilon}) } ) query time (for a query curve of length m), where the similarity between two curves is their discrete Fr\'echet or dynamic time warping distance. Our approach consists of a discretization of space based on the input curves, which allows us to prepare a small set of curves that captures all possible queries approximately. Our method is simple and deterministic, yet, somewhat surprisingly, it is more efficient than all previous methods. We also apply our method to a version of approximate range counting for curves and achieve similar bounds.
ref:
In the \((1+\varepsilon,r)\)-approximate near-neighbor problem for curves (ANNC) with distance measure \(\delta\), we build a data structure for a given set \(\mathcal{C}\) of curves. Given a query curve \(Q\), if some curve \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) satisfies \(\delta(Q,C)\le r\), the data structure returns a curve \(C'\in\mathcal{C}\) such that \(\delta(Q,C')\le(1+\varepsilon)r\).

The \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate nearest-neighbor problem can be reduced efficiently to ANNC. In that problem, a query returns a curve \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) such that \(\delta(Q,C)\le(1+\varepsilon)\delta(Q,C^*)\), where \(C^*\) is the curve in \(\mathcal{C}\) closest to \(Q\).

Given \(n\) curves, each with \(m\) points in \(d\) dimensions, we build an ANNC data structure that uses \(n\cdot O(1/\varepsilon)^{md}\) storage and answers queries in \(O\!\left(md\log(nm/\varepsilon)\right)\) time for query curves of length \(m\). The distance between two curves may be either discrete Fréchet distance or dynamic time warping distance.

Our approach discretizes the space based on the input curves. This lets us prepare a small set of curves that approximately captures every possible query. The method is simple and deterministic but, somewhat surprisingly, more efficient than every previous method. We also apply it to a version of approximate range counting for curves and obtain similar bounds.

source: Cell movement in the early phase of C. elegans development is regulated by a highly complex process in which a set of rules and connections are formulated at distinct scales. Previous efforts have demonstrated that agent-based, multi-scale modeling systems can integrate physical and biological rules and provide new avenues to study developmental systems. However, the application of these systems to model cell movement is still challenging and requires a comprehensive understanding of regulation networks at the right scales. Recent developments in deep learning and reinforcement learning provide an unprecedented opportunity to explore cell movement using 3D time-lapse microscopy images. We presented a deep reinforcement learning approach within an agent-based modeling system to characterize cell movement in the embryonic development of C. elegans . We tested our model through two scenarios within real developmental processes: the anterior movement of the Cpaaa cell via intercalation and the restoration of the superficial left-right symmetry. Our modeling system overcame the local optimization problems encountered by traditional rule-based, agent-based modeling by using greedy algorithms. It also overcame the computational challenges in the action selection which has been plagued by the traditional tabular-based reinforcement learning approach. Our system can automatically explore the cell movement path by using live microscopy images and it can provide a unique capability to model cell movement scenarios where regulatory mechanisms are not well studied. In addition, our system can be used to explore potential paths of a cell under different regulatory mechanisms or to facilitate new hypotheses for explaining certain cell movement behaviors .
ref: A complex process regulates cell movement early in C. elegans development, establishing rules and connections at different scales. Previous studies have shown that agent-based, multiscale modeling systems can combine physical and biological rules and offer new ways to study development. However, using these systems to model cell movement remains difficult and requires a thorough understanding of regulatory networks at the appropriate scales. Recent advances in deep learning and reinforcement learning offer an unprecedented opportunity to study cell movement with 3D time-lapse microscopy images. We presented a deep reinforcement learning method within an agent-based modeling system to describe cell movement during C. elegans embryonic development. We tested the model in two real developmental scenarios: the Cpaaa cell’s anterior movement through intercalation and the restoration of superficial left-right symmetry. By using greedy algorithms, our modeling system avoided the local optimization problems found in traditional rule-based, agent-based modeling. It also addressed the computational difficulty of selecting actions that has hindered traditional tabular reinforcement learning. Using live microscopy images, our system can automatically explore a cell’s movement path and can model cell movement when the regulatory mechanisms are not well understood. It can also explore possible cell paths under different regulatory mechanisms or help develop new hypotheses to explain specific cell movement behaviors.

source: Nested sampling is a technique developed to explore probability distributions localised in an exponentially small area of the parameter space. The algorithm provides both posterior samples and an estimate of the evidence (marginal likelihood) of the model. Previous applications of the algorithm have yielded large efficiency gains over other sampling techniques  including parallel tempering. In this paper we apply the nested sampling algorithm to the problem of protein folding in a  force field of empirical potentials that were designed to stabilize secondary structure elements in room-temperature simulations. A topological analysis of the posterior samples is performed to produce energy landscape charts, which give a high level description of the potential energy surface for the protein folding simulations. These charts provide qualitative insights into both the folding process and the nature of the model and force field used.  The topology of the protein molecule emerges as a major determinant of the shape of the energy landscape . The algorithm was tested with protein G. The tertiary structure of the protein was predicted to a reasonably high level of accuracy. The best conformation found had an RMSD of 3.12A from the native structure. Two other proteins, chymotrypsin inhibitor 2 and Src tyrosine kinase SH3 domain, were also tested, with the best conformations found having RMSD 4.75A and 5.33A from their respective native structures . The nested sampling algorithm also provides an efficient way to calculate free energies and the expectation value of thermodynamic observables at any temperature, through a simple post-processing of the output.
ref:
Nested sampling was developed to explore probability distributions confined to an exponentially small region of parameter space. The algorithm produces posterior samples and estimates the model evidence, or marginal likelihood. Previous uses have shown large efficiency gains over other sampling methods, including parallel tempering.

In this paper, we apply nested sampling to protein folding using a force field of empirical potentials designed to stabilize secondary-structure elements in room-temperature simulations. We analyze the topology of the posterior samples to create energy landscape charts. These charts give a high-level view of the potential energy surface in the protein-folding simulations and provide qualitative insight into the folding process and the model and force field used. The protein molecule’s topology emerges as a major factor shaping the energy landscape.

We tested the algorithm on protein G and predicted its tertiary structure with reasonably high accuracy. The best conformation had an RMSD of 3.12 Å from the native structure. We also tested chymotrypsin inhibitor 2 and the Src tyrosine kinase SH3 domain. Their best conformations had RMSDs of 4.75 Å and 5.33 Å from their respective native structures.

Nested sampling also provides an efficient way to calculate free energies and the expected values of thermodynamic observables at any temperature through simple post-processing of the output.

source: Modern digital electronics support remarkably reliable computing, especially given the challenge of controlling nanoscale logical components that interact in fluctuating environments. However,  the high-reliability limit is subject to a fundamental error-energy-efficiency tradeoff that arises from time-symmetric control . Requiring a low probability of error causes energy consumption to diverge as logarithm of the inverse error rate for nonreciprocal logical transitions. The reciprocity (self-invertibility) of a computation is a stricter condition for thermodynamic efficiency than logical reversibility (invertibility), the latter being the root of Landauer's work bound . In fact, the average energy required for reliable erasure is well above that bound. Explicit simulations of work production closely track the error-dissipation tradeoff , diverging from the Landauer bound as the error rate decreases. And, unlike the Landauer work, which can be recovered, the nonreciprocal work must be irreversibly dissipated. Analogous bounds hold for the universal NAND gate and extend to circuits of logical gates. That said, strictly-reciprocal logic gates, such as communication relays and NOT gates, are exempt and can be efficiently implemented via time-symmetric protocols. For all other computations, though, time-asymmetric control must be used to avoid dissipation arising from nonreciprocity. The lesson is that highly-reliable computation under time-symmetric control cannot reach, and is often far above, the Landauer limit. In this way, time-asymmetry becomes a design principle for thermodynamically-efficient computing. We also demonstrate that the time-reversal symmetries of the memory elements themselves play an essential role in determining the minimal energy necessary to implement a computation .

source: Chemical reaction networks taken with mass-action kinetics are dynamical systems that arise in chemical engineering and systems biology. Deciding whether a chemical reaction network admits multiple positive steady states is to determine existence of multiple positive solutions to a system of polynomials with unknown coefficients. In this work, we consider the question of whether the minimal (in a precise sense)  networks, which we propose to call `atoms of multistationarity,' characterize the entire set of multistationary networks. We show that if a subnetwork admits multiple nondegenerate positive steady states, then these steady states can be extended to establish multistationarity of a larger network, provided that the two networks share the same stoichiometric subspace. Our result provides the mathematical foundation for a technique used by Siegal-Gaskins et al. of establishing bistability by way of `network ancestry.' Here, our main application is for enumerating small multistationary continuous-flow stirred-tank reactors (CFSTRs), which are networks in which all chemical species take part in the inflow and outflow. Recent work of the first author presented a simple characterization of the one-reaction CFSTRs that admit multiple positive steady states. Here we consider the two-reaction CFSTRs. We enumerate all 386 bimolecular and reversible such networks. Of these, exactly 35 admit multiple positive steady states. Moreover, each admits a unique minimal multistationary subnetwork, and these subnetworks form a poset (with respect to the relation of `removing species') which has 11 minimal elements  .
ref:
Chemical reaction networks with mass-action kinetics are dynamical systems found in chemical engineering and systems biology. Deciding whether a network has multiple positive steady states means determining whether a system of polynomials with unknown coefficients has multiple positive solutions. We ask whether the minimal networks, in a precise sense, characterize all multistationary networks. We call these minimal networks “atoms of multistationarity.” We show that when a subnetwork has multiple nondegenerate positive steady states, these states can be extended to prove that a larger network is multistationary, provided both networks have the same stoichiometric subspace. This result gives a mathematical basis for the “network ancestry” technique that Siegal-Gaskins et al. used to establish bistability.

Our main application is to enumerate small multistationary continuous-flow stirred-tank reactors (CFSTRs), networks in which every chemical species participates in inflow and outflow. Recent work by the first author gave a simple characterization of one-reaction CFSTRs that have multiple positive steady states. Here, we study two-reaction CFSTRs. We enumerate all 386 such networks that are bimolecular and reversible. Exactly 35 have multiple positive steady states. Each also has a unique minimal multistationary subnetwork. Under the relation of “removing species,” these subnetworks form a partially ordered set with 11 minimal elements.

source: Credit (CVA), Debit (DVA) and Funding Valuation Adjustments (FVA) are now familiar valuation adjustments made to the value of a portfolio of derivatives to account for credit risks and funding costs. However, recent changes in the regulatory regime and the increases in regulatory capital requirements has led many banks to include the cost of capital in derivative pricing. This paper formalises the addition of cost of capital by extending the Burgard-Kjaer  semi-replication approach to CVA and FVA to include an addition capital term, Capital Valuation Adjustment (KVA, i.e. Kapital Valuation Adjustment to distinguish from CVA . Two approaches are considered, one where the (regulatory) capital is released back to shareholders upon counterparty default and one where the capital can be used to offset losses in the event of counterparty default  . The use of the semi-replication approach means that the flexibility around the treatment of self-default is carried over into this analysis. The paper further considers the practical calculation of KVA with reference to the Basel II (BCBS-128) and Basel III (BCBS-189) Capital regimes and its implementation via CRD IV (CRD-IV-Regulation,CRD-IV-Directive) . The paper assesses how KVA may be hedged, given that any hedging transactions themselves would lead to regulatory capital requirements and hence KVA. To conclude, a number of numerical examples are presented to gauge the cost impact of KVA on vanilla derivative products.
ref:
Credit (CVA), debit (DVA), and funding valuation adjustments (FVA) are now common adjustments to derivative portfolio values that account for credit risks and funding costs. However, recent regulatory changes and higher capital requirements have led many banks to include the cost of capital in derivative prices.

This paper formalises that cost by extending the Burgard-Kjaer semi-replication approach to CVA and FVA with an additional capital term: Capital Valuation Adjustment, or KVA (“Kapital” Valuation Adjustment, to distinguish it from CVA). It considers two approaches. In one, regulatory capital returns to shareholders when a counterparty defaults. In the other, the capital can offset losses caused by counterparty default.

Because the paper uses semi-replication, it retains flexibility in how it treats the bank’s own default. It also examines how to calculate KVA in practice under the Basel II (BCBS-128) and Basel III (BCBS-189) capital regimes and their implementation through CRD IV (CRD-IV-Regulation and CRD-IV-Directive).

The paper assesses how banks may hedge KVA, given that the hedging transactions would themselves create regulatory capital requirements and therefore KVA. Finally, it presents several numerical examples to measure KVA’s cost impact on vanilla derivative products.

source: This paper proposes a model of financial contagion that accounts for explosive, mutually exciting shocks to market volatility. We fit the model using country-level data during the European sovereign debt crisis, which has its roots in the period 2008--2010, and was continuing to affect global markets as of October, 2011. Our analysis shows that existing volatility models are unable to explain two key stylized features of global markets during presumptive contagion periods: shocks to aggregate market volatility can be sudden and explosive, and they are associated with specific directional biases in the cross-section of country-level returns. Our model repairs this deficit by assuming that the random shocks to volatility are heavy-tailed and correlated cross-sectionally, both with each other and with returns. We find evidence for significant contagion effects during the major EU crisis periods of May 2010 and August 2011, where contagion is defined as excess correlation in the residuals from a factor model incorporating global and regional market risk factors. Some of this excess correlation can be explained by quantifying the impact of shocks to aggregate volatility in the cross-section of expected returns---but only, it turns out, if one is extremely careful in accounting for the explosive nature of these shocks. We show that global markets have time-varying cross-sectional sensitivities to these shocks, and that high sensitivities strongly predict periods of financial crisis. Moreover, the pattern of temporal changes in correlation structure between volatility and returns is readily interpretable in terms of the major events of the periods in question.
ref:
This paper presents a model of financial contagion that captures explosive shocks to market volatility that reinforce one another. We fit the model to country-level data from the European sovereign debt crisis, which began in 2008–2010 and was still affecting global markets in October 2011.

Our analysis shows that existing volatility models cannot explain two key patterns in global markets during presumed periods of contagion. Shocks to overall market volatility can be sudden and explosive, and they are linked to specific directional biases across country-level returns.

Our model addresses this weakness by assuming that random volatility shocks have heavy tails and are correlated across countries, both with one another and with returns. We find evidence of significant contagion during the major EU crisis periods of May 2010 and August 2011. We define contagion as excess correlation in the residuals of a factor model that includes global and regional market risk factors.

We can explain some of this excess correlation by measuring how shocks to overall volatility affect expected returns across countries—but only if we account with extreme care for the explosive nature of those shocks. We show that global markets’ cross-sectional sensitivity to these shocks changes over time, and that high sensitivity strongly predicts periods of financial crisis. The way correlations between volatility and returns change over time can also be readily understood in light of the major events during the periods studied.

source: Tuning curves characterizing the response selectivities of biological neurons often exhibit large degrees of irregularity and diversity across neurons. Theoretical network models that feature heterogeneous cell populations or random connectivity also generate diverse tuning behaviors across cells . However, a general framework for fitting such models to experimentally measured tuning curves is lacking. We address this problem by proposing to view mechanistic network models as generative models whose parameters can be optimized to fit the distribution of experimentally measured tuning curves. A major obstacle for fitting such models is that , in most cases of interest, an explicit form for the likelihood function , i.e. the distribution of generated tuning curves, is not available . Recent advances in machine learning provide ways for fitting generative models without the need to evaluate the likelihood and its gradient. Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) provide one such framework , and have been successful in traditional machine learning tasks. We apply this approach in two separate experiments, showing how GANs can be used to fit commonly used mechanistic models in theoretical neuroscience to datasets of measured tuning curves. This approach avoids the computationally expensive step of inferring latent variables, e.g. the biophysical parameters of individual cells or the particular realization of the full synaptic connectivity matrix, and directly learns model parameters which characterize the statistics of connectivity or  single-cell properties. Another strength of this approach is that it fits the entire, joint distribution of experimental tuning curves, instead of matching a few summary statistics picked  by the user. This framework opens the door to fitting theoretically motivated dynamical network models directly to simultaneously or non-simultaneously recorded neural responses.

Recent advances in machine learning make it possible to fit generative models without evaluating the likelihood or its gradient. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) offer one such method and have succeeded in traditional machine learning tasks. We apply this method in two separate experiments and show how GANs can fit commonly used mechanistic models in theoretical neuroscience to datasets of measured tuning curves. The method avoids the costly task of inferring latent variables, such as the biophysical parameters of individual cells or a specific realization of the full synaptic connectivity matrix. Instead, it directly learns model parameters that describe the statistics of connectivity or single-cell properties. It also fits the full joint distribution of experimental tuning curves rather than matching a few summary statistics chosen by the user. This framework makes it possible to fit theoretically motivated dynamical network models directly to neural responses recorded either simultaneously or at different times.

source: We develop new procedures to quantify the statistical uncertainty from sorting units in panel data into groups using data-driven clustering algorithms. In our  setting, each unit belongs to one of a finite number of latent groups and its regression curve is determined by which group it belongs to. Our main contribution is a new joint confidence set for group membership. Each element of the joint confidence set is a vector of possible group assignments for all units. The vector of true group memberships is contained in the confidence set with a pre-specified probability . The confidence set inverts a test for group membership . This test exploits a characterization of the true group memberships by a system of moment inequalities. Our procedure solves a high-dimensional one-sided testing problem and tests group membership simultaneously for all units. We also propose a procedure for identifying units for which group membership is obviously determined. These units can be ignored when computing critical values. We justify the joint confidence set under N, T \to \infty asymptotics where we allow T to be much smaller than N. Our arguments rely on the theory of self-normalized sums and high-dimensional central limit theorems. We contribute new theoretical results for testing problems with a large number of moment inequalities, including an anti-concentration inequality for the quasi-likelihood ratio (QLR ) statistic . Monte Carlo results indicate that our confidence set has adequate coverage and is informative. We illustrate the practical relevance of our confidence set in two applications.

source: The Mapper produces a compact summary of high dimensional data as a simplicial complex. We study the problem of quantifying the interestingness of subpopulations in a Mapper, which appear as long paths, flares, or loops. First, we create a weighted directed graph G using the 1-skeleton of the Mapper. We use the average values at the vertices of a target function to direct edges (from low to high). The difference between the average values at vertices (high-low) is set as its weight. Covariation of the remaining h functions (independent variables) is captured by a h-bit binary signature assigned to the edge. An interesting path in G is a directed path whose edges all have the same signature. We define the interestingness score of such a path as a sum of its edge weights multiplied by a nonlinear function of their ranks in the path. Second, we study three optimization problems on this graph G. In the problem Max-IP, we seek an interesting path in G with the maximum interestingness score. We show that Max-IP is NP-complete. For the special case when G is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), we show that Max-IP can be solved in polynomial time - in O(mnd_i) where d_i is the maximum indegree of a vertex in G. In the more general problem IP, the goal is to find a collection of  interesting paths such that these paths form an exact cover of E (hence they are edge-disjoint) and the overall sum of interestingness scores of all paths is maximized. We also study a variant of IP termed k-IP, where the goal is to identify a collection of edge-disjoint interesting paths each with k edges, and the total interestingness score of all paths is maximized. While k-IP can be solved in polynomial time for k <= 2, we show k-IP is NP-complete for k >= 3. Further, we show that k-IP remains NP-complete for k >= 3 even for the case when G is a DAG. We develop polynomial time heuristics for IP and k-IP on DAGs.

Mapper summarizes high-dimensional data as a compact simplicial complex. We study how to measure the interestingness of subpopulations in a Mapper that appear as long paths, flares, or loops.

First, we build a weighted directed graph \(G\) from the Mapper’s 1-skeleton. We direct each edge from the vertex with the lower average target-function value to the vertex with the higher value. The edge weight is the difference between these average values. To capture how the remaining \(h\) functions—the independent variables—vary together, we assign each edge an \(h\)-bit binary signature. An interesting path in \(G\) is a directed path whose edges all have the same signature. Its interestingness score is the sum of its edge weights, each multiplied by a nonlinear function of its rank in the path.

Second, we study three optimization problems on \(G\). In Max-IP, we seek the interesting path with the highest interestingness score. We show that Max-IP is NP-complete. When \(G\) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), however, Max-IP can be solved in polynomial time: \(O(mnd_i)\), where \(d_i\) is the maximum indegree of any vertex in \(G\).

In the more general IP problem, we seek a collection of interesting paths that exactly covers \(E\), so the paths are edge-disjoint, while maximizing the sum of their interestingness scores. We also study a variant called \(k\)-IP. Its goal is to find a collection of edge-disjoint interesting paths, each with \(k\) edges, that maximizes the total interestingness score. Although \(k\)-IP can be solved in polynomial time when \(k \leq 2\), we show that it is NP-complete when \(k \geq 3\). It remains NP-complete for \(k \geq 3\) even when \(G\) is a DAG. We develop polynomial-time heuristics for IP and \(k\)-IP on DAGs.

“Hunting should be about fair chase ... testing the wits of a hunter against that of the animal,” he told a press conference. “Over the years that got eroded and now we are trying to re-establish that principle.”

Sage Dadhichi raised Saraswata after finding him as a child floating in the Saraswati River. Indra, king of the Devas, had a weapon called the Vajra made from Dadhichi’s skeleton and used it against his enemies, the Asuras. One of them happened to find Saraswata, the foremost of sages, reading the Vedas with full attention. He returned to the gathering of rishis and told them about Saraswata, who had unrivalled splendour and a godlike form and was reading the Vedas alone in a forest.

Gesture music

Silence in music happens when the music stops during a performance. Gesture music sometimes replaces it.

Sofia Gubaidulina

In *Sofia Gubaidulina: A Biography*, Michael Kurtz mentions the conductor’s silent solo performance in *...Stimmenn... verstummen...*, a 1986 orchestral work. (Michael Kurtz, *Sofia Gubaidulina: A Biography*, p. 184, written in 2001, English translation, Indiana University Press, 2007.)

Milan Knizak

From 1960, the International Fluxus Movement created Events or Verbal Pieces. Their time structures were usually vague, sometimes with no beginning or end. They could include sound or music, or neither. One striking example is Czech artist Milan Knizak’s 1965 *Snowstorm N1*. Its score says: “Paper gliders are distributed to an idle and waiting audience.”

Helmut Lachenmann

In 1977, Lachenmann composed *Salut Fr Caldwell* for two guitars. The piece includes silent moments when “the players’ silent motions and gestures created a space of unheard music.” (Michael Kurtz, *Sofia Gubaidulina: A Biography*, p. 192, written in 2001, English translation, Indiana University Press, 2007.)

Takehisa Kosugi

In 1963, Takehisa Kosugi composed a piece called *Theatre Music* for *Fluxus 1*. It took the form of a cardstock rectangle bearing the trace of feet moving in a spiral. The instructions said: “Keep walking intently.” (Charles Mereweather, ed., *Art Anti-Art Non-Art*, Getty Research Institute, 2007, p. 21.)

Juan Mara Solare

His *Gestenstcke* (2008) is a collection of five pieces for four performers. It uses musical structure to organize non-sounding elements, specifically gestures. For example, the cycle’s first piece is a canon of gestures. Ensemble Neues Musiktheater premiered it at the University of Bremen on June 12, 2008.

Another non-sounding piece is his 2013 conceptual work *Tense Atmosphere*, a graphic score consisting of a silence with a sforzato sign.

The optophonic piano

Wladimir Baranoff-Rossin began building his optophonic piano in the 1915s. (See Baranoff-Rossin’s official web page.) A small keyboard rotates a set of painted glass discs. Light shines through the discs and onto a wall. The player can control the light’s intensity and the discs’ rotation speed. Six or eight keys on the three-octave keyboard control colored discs.

It is unclear what kind of sound the keyboard can produce. Oscillator frequencies, as some articles claim, are rather unlikely between 1915 and 1920. More likely, piano accompaniment accompanied the light show, perhaps played on the Optosonic Piano’s reduced keyboard, which resembled a toy piano.

Unfinished or abandoned music

At one point, music exists in the composer’s mind. In 1928, Edgard Varse began work on an opera called *L’Astronome*, based on North American Indian legends. He never finished it and destroyed the drafts.

In 1932, he asked Antonin Artaud to write the libretto for a large-scale oratorio, *Il n’ya plus de firmament* (*There Is No Longer Any Firmament*). In *Phantasmatic Radio*, Allen S. Weiss translates the opening of Artaud’s text:

“Darkness. Explosions in this darkness. Harmonies suddenly broken off. Harsh sounds. Depressurized soundings. The music will give the impression of a distant cataclysm and will fill the room, falling as from vertiginous heights.”

Finger bowl from the 1880s

A finger bowl holds water that dinner guests use to rinse their fingers. At a formal meal served *la russe*, it is brought to the table with the final course, either dessert or fruit. At a less formal meal, it may be served after any course that includes finger food and may appear after more than one such course.

Formal service

The finger bowl usually arrives with the dessert plate. Before dessert is served, the guest moves it to the upper left. After dessert, guests dip their fingers into the water and dry them with their napkins.

In formal service, the finger bowl usually sits on a linen doily on the dessert plate, with the dessert fork and spoon on either side. Each guest moves the flatware to the sides of the dessert plate and places the finger bowl and doily at the plate’s upper left. “This is the only time during a formal meal that a guest takes part in placing the appointments for a course.”

If a separate fruit course follows dessert, the finger bowl arrives with the fruit plate, fork, and knife, arranged as they would be on a dessert plate. Another option is to bring all the dessert and fruit dishes at once. The finger bowl sits on the dessert plate with its fork and spoon, and the dessert plate sits on the fruit plate, with doilies between the dishes. With this service, the fruit fork and knife arrive after the dessert plates and silverware have been cleared.

After dessert, or after fruit if it is served as a separate course, guests lightly dip their fingertips into the water, one hand at a time, then wipe them on the napkin in their lap.

Johnson, 38, of Kingsford, Michigan was charged on Wednesday with killing three teenagers in a shooting on the Menominee River near Niagara, Wisconsin. Johnson was charged with first-degree intentional homicide. Authorities say he went to the popular bathing spot near the East Kingsford Railroad Bridge on July 31 and opened fire with a military-style rifle, killing three and injuring one. The Associated Press reports that he faces life in prison without parole if convicted . Wisconsin does not have the death penalty. However, as one of the bodies was found on the Michigan side of the border, he could potentially face charges there, or perhaps even in federal court. He is being represented by a public defender, Len Kachinsky. Local teens said Johnson often was seen at the site, but mostly kept to himself. On July 31, the Associated Press reports  he emerged from the woods wearing camouflage clothing and opened fire without saying a word. Johnson fled and surrendered the next day after a multi-agency manhunt. Johnson had been accused of a sexual assault, and his mother speculated he may have panicked after hearing police wanted to speak with him. The Detroit Free Press reports that  in a confession to police, Johnson said the shooting was set in motion when Johnson lured the woman to the bridge the day before and sexually assaulted her. Worried that he would be arrested, Johnson returned to the woods, planning to ambush law enforcement officers coming to find him. After he spent a night in the woods and no officers came, he returned home at 10 a.m.  on July 31, asked his mother if police had been looking for him, then left at 3:00 p.m. He says he then got his weapons and returned to the woods. Johnson said he planned to wait for the teens to reach the Michigan side of the river so he could kill them all and use them as "bait" to lure police into his ambush. However, Spigarelli and Pohlson unexpectedly approached his position, and he said he felt trapped and he opened fire. Spigarelli and Pohlson were both shot in the head and died instantly. Johnson then reloaded and fired across the river, killing Bryan Mort.

source: The occurrence of drug-drug-interactions (DDI) from multiple drug dispensations is a serious problem, both for individuals and health-care systems, since patients with complications due to DDI are likely to re-enter the system at a costlier level. We present a large-scale longitudinal study (18 months) of the DDI phenomenon at the primary- and secondary-care level using electronic health records (EHR) from the city of Blumenau in Southern Brazil (pop. ~ 340,000). This is the first study of DDI we are aware of that follows an entire city longitudinally for more than 3 months. We found that 181 distinct drug pairs known to interact were dispensed concomitantly to 12 \% of the patients in the city's public health-care system. Further, 4\% of the patients were dispensed DDI combinations, likely to result in major adverse reactions with costs estimated to be larger than previously reported in smaller studies. DDI results are integrated into associative networks for inference and visualization, revealing key medications and interactions involved in the DDI phenomenon. Analysis reveals that women have a 60\% increased risk of DDI as compared to men; the increase becomes 90\% when only major DDI are considered. Furthermore, DDI risk increases substantially with age. Patients aged 70-79 years have a 34\% risk of DDI when they are dispensed two or more drugs concomitantly. Interestingly, a null model demonstrates that age- and women-specific risks from increased polypharmacy fail by far to explain the observed risks of DDI in those populations. This suggests that social and biological factors are at play. These results demonstrate that considerable gender and age biases exist, but that accurate warning systems for known DDI can be devised for health-care systems and public-health policy management, to reduce DDI-related adverse reactions and health-care costs. \\%DIF > of the patients in the city's public health-care system. ref:
Drug-drug interactions (DDI) caused by dispensing multiple drugs are a serious problem for patients and health-care systems. Patients with DDI complications are likely to return to the system needing more costly care.

We conducted a large, 18-month study of DDI in primary and secondary care using electronic health records from Blumenau, a city of about 340,000 people in southern Brazil. To our knowledge, this is the first DDI study to track an entire city for more than three months.

In the city’s public health-care system, 12% of patients received, at the same time, drugs from 181 distinct pairs known to interact. In addition, 4% received DDI combinations likely to cause major adverse reactions, with estimated costs higher than those previously reported in smaller studies.

We integrated the DDI results into associative networks for analysis and visualization. These networks identified the main drugs and interactions involved. The analysis found that women had a 60% higher risk of DDI than men. For major DDI alone, their risk was 90% higher. DDI risk also rose substantially with age. Among patients aged 70–79 who received two or more drugs at the same time, 34% were at risk of DDI.

A null model showed that greater use of multiple drugs among women and older people fell far short of explaining their observed DDI risks. This suggests that social and biological factors also play a role.

These results show substantial gender and age biases. They also show that health-care systems and public-health managers can create accurate warning systems for known DDI to reduce related adverse reactions and costs.

In addition, 4% of patients received drug pairs likely to cause major adverse drug reactions (ADR), with estimated costs much higher than those previously reported in smaller studies. The large-scale analysis found that women had a 60% higher risk of DDI than men and a 90% higher risk when the analysis included only DDI known to cause major ADR. DDI risk also rose substantially with age. Among patients aged 70–79 who received two or more drugs at the same time, 34% were at risk of DDI.

A statistical null model showed that greater use of multiple drugs among women and older people fell far short of explaining their observed DDI risks, suggesting unknown social or biological causes. We also provide a network visualization of the drugs and demographic factors that define the DDI problem. The results show that health-care and public-health managers can use accurate DDI prediction to reduce DDI-related ADR and costs.

source: In economic and financial networks, the strength (total value of the connections) of a given node has always an important economic meaning, such as the size of supply and demand, import and export, or financial exposure. Constructing null models of networks matching the observed strengths of all nodes is crucial in order to either detect interesting deviations of an empirical network from economically meaningful benchmarks or reconstruct the most likely structure of an economic network when the latter is unknown. However, several studies have proved that real economic networks  are topologically very different from networks inferred only from node strengths. Here we provide a detailed analysis for the World Trade Web (WTW) by comparing it to an enhanced null model that simultaneously reproduces the strength and the number of connections of each node. We study several temporal snapshots and different aggregation levels (commodity classes) of the WTW and systematically find that the observed properties are extremely well reproduced by our model. This allows us to introduce the concept of extensive and intensive bias, defined as a measurable tendency of the network to prefer either the formation of new links or the reinforcement of existing ones.
ref: In economic and financial networks, a node’s strength—the total value of its connections—always has an important economic meaning, such as the size of supply and demand, imports and exports, or financial exposure. Building network null models that match the observed strengths of all nodes is crucial for detecting meaningful differences between a real network and economic benchmarks, or for reconstructing the most likely structure of an economic network when its structure is unknown. However, several studies have proved that real economic networks have very different structures from networks inferred only from node strengths. We provide a detailed analysis of the World Trade Web (WTW), comparing it with an enhanced null model that reproduces both the strength and the number of connections of each node. We study several points in time and different levels of WTW aggregation, or commodity classes, and consistently find that our model reproduces the observed properties extremely well. This result lets us introduce the concepts of extensive and intensive bias, defined as a measurable tendency for a network to favor either forming new links or strengthening existing ones.

source: Cardiovascular waveforms contain information for clinical diagnosis. By "learning" URLanizing the subtle change of waveform morphology from large amounts of raw waveform data, unsupervised manifold learning can help delineate a high-dimensional structure . We hypothesize that the shape of this structure conveys inner dynamics information via the novel three-dimensional (3D) image. To validate this hypothesis, we investigate the electrocardiography (ECG) waveform for ischemic heart disease and arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveform in dynamic vasoactive episodes. For non-ST-elevation ECG obtained from public database, a classification tree structure comprising consecutive ECG waveforms spanning from unstable angina to healthy control is presented . Support vector machine (SVM) shows classification accuracyof 99.8\%. Manifold learning in ST-elevation ECG waveform analysis helps quantify the evolving direction of  ST-elevation myocardial episode in a 1-hour period  . The ABP waveform analysis of Nicardipine administration shows inter-individual difference ( SVM classification accuracy= 99.3\% ) and their common directions from intra-individual moving trajectories. The dynamic change of  ABP waveform during endo-tracheal intubation shows a loop-like trajectory structure, which can be further classified using the knowledge of antihypertensive medication. The application of manifold learning in ECG and ABP waveform analysis provides clues of acute coronary syndrome diagnosis, predicts clinical course in myocardial ischemic episode and reveals underneath physiological mechanism via 3D visualization .
ref:
Cardiovascular waveforms contain information that can support clinical diagnosis. Unsupervised manifold learning can map a high-dimensional structure by “learning” URLanizing subtle changes in waveform shape from large amounts of raw data. We hypothesize that the shape of this structure conveys information about internal dynamics through a novel three-dimensional (3D) image. To test this hypothesis, we study electrocardiography (ECG) waveforms in ischemic heart disease and arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms during dynamic vasoactive episodes.

For non-ST-elevation ECG data from a public database, we present a classification tree of consecutive ECG waveforms ranging from unstable angina to healthy controls. A support vector machine (SVM) achieves 99.8% classification accuracy. In ST-elevation ECG analysis, manifold learning helps quantify how a ST-elevation myocardial episode evolves over one hour. Analysis of ABP waveforms during nicardipine administration shows differences among individuals, with 99.3% SVM classification accuracy, as well as shared directions in each individual’s moving trajectories. Dynamic changes in ABP waveforms during endotracheal intubation form a loop-like trajectory that can be further classified using information about antihypertensive medication. Applying manifold learning to ECG and ABP waveforms provides clues for diagnosing acute coronary syndrome, predicts the clinical course of myocardial ischemic episodes, and uses 3D visualization to reveal underlying physiological mechanisms.

source: When simulating a complex stochastic system, the behavior of the output response depends on the input parameters estimated from finite real-world data, and the finiteness of data brings input uncertainty to the output response . The quantification of the impact of input uncertainty on output response has been extensively studied. Most of the existing literature focuses on providing inferences on the mean output response with respect to input uncertainty , including point estimation and confidence interval construction of the mean response. However, risk assessment of the mean response with respect to input uncertainty often plays an important role in system evaluation /controlbecause it quantifies the behavior of the mean response under extreme input models. To the best of our knowledge, it has been rarely systematically studied in the literature. In the present paper, we will fill in the gap and introduce risk measures for input uncertaintyin output analysis. We develop nested Monte Carlo estimators and construct (asymptotically valid) confidence intervals for risk measures of mean response. We further study the associated budget allocation problem for more efficient nested simulation of the estimators, and propose a novel method to solve the problem .
ref: When simulating a complex stochastic system, the output depends on input parameters estimated from finite real-world data. Because the data are finite, they create input uncertainty in the output. Researchers have studied the effects of input uncertainty on output extensively. Most studies focus on inferences about the mean output response under input uncertainty, including point estimates and confidence intervals. However, assessing the risk of the mean response under input uncertainty often matters for system evaluation and control because it shows how the mean response behaves under extreme input models. To the best of our knowledge, the literature has rarely studied this topic systematically. This paper fills that gap by introducing risk measures for input uncertainty in output analysis. We develop nested Monte Carlo estimators and construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals for risk measures of the mean response. We also study how to allocate the budget for more efficient nested simulation of the estimators and propose a new method for solving this problem.

source: We analyze total, asymmetric and frequency connectedness between the oil and forex markets using high-frequency  intra-day data over  2007 -- 2015. Methodologically, we extend the Diebold-Yilmaz spillover index in two ways to account for asymmetric and frequency connectedness . Empirically, our resultsshow that by combining crude oil with the set of currencies a total connectedness of the portfolio is lower than the total connectedness of the forex market itself. Further, in terms of asymmetries we show that bad volatility dominates connectedness on the forex market. However, when we add oil into a hypothetical portfolio of oil and foreign currencies, asymmetry in connectedness between the two classes of assets reverses in favor of the good volatility. Finally, the frequency connectedness analysis reveals that dynamic of the shorter and longer term connectedness dramatically differs. While shorter-term connectedness is usually low, the long-term connectedness sharply rises during the global financial crisis, European debt crisis, and after the oil price drop in 2014. Hence, the long-term connectedness reflects worrisome beliefs of investors and correlates with the increased market uncertainty .
ref: We analyze total, asymmetric, and frequency connectedness between oil and foreign exchange markets using high-frequency intraday data from 2007 to 2015. We extend the Diebold-Yilmaz spillover index in two ways to measure asymmetric and frequency connectedness. Our results show that a portfolio combining crude oil and currencies has lower total connectedness than the foreign exchange market alone. We also show that bad volatility drives connectedness in the foreign exchange market. However, when we add oil to a hypothetical portfolio of oil and foreign currencies, the asymmetry in connectedness between the two asset classes reverses, with good volatility dominating. The frequency analysis shows that short- and long-term connectedness change very differently. Short-term connectedness is usually low, while long-term connectedness rises sharply during the global financial crisis, the European debt crisis, and after the 2014 oil price drop. Long-term connectedness therefore reflects investors’ concerns and correlates with greater market uncertainty.

source: During asymmetric cell divisions, cortical dyneins generate forcesessential to position the spindle after polarity cues, prescribing daughter cells fate. In nematode zygote, cortical dynein pulls on microtubules transiently, raising the question of its targeting and dynamics. Tracking and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy revealed that in the cytoplasm, dynein spots displayed directed motions toward the cortex, localized at microtubule plus-ends through EBP-2 / EB but are not actively transported. Surprisingly CLIP-1/CLIP170 is not involved. ebp-2(0) slightly reduced spindle rocking, thus most cortical forcesremain suggesting a redundant mechanism . At the cortex, to relate dynein residency and forces generating, we tracked dynein and found two dynamically distinct populations. One of them would correspond to force generating events. Our experiments also indicated that an asymmetric (polarized) dynein-microbutule on-rate, causes the force imbalance positioning the spindle. GPR-1/2 increases the overall dynein density but also residency time (pulling processivity), although this latter was not polarized .
ref: During asymmetric cell division, cortical dynein generates forces that position the spindle in response to polarity cues, determining daughter cell fate. In the nematode zygote, cortical dynein pulls briefly on microtubules, raising questions about how it reaches the cortex and behaves there. Tracking and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy showed that dynein spots in the cytoplasm moved toward the cortex. They localized at microtubule plus ends through EBP-2/EB but were not actively transported. Surprisingly, CLIP-1/CLIP170 was not involved. Loss of EBP-2 slightly reduced spindle rocking, so most cortical forces remained, suggesting a redundant mechanism. To link dynein’s time at the cortex with force generation, we tracked dynein and found two populations with different dynamics. One population would correspond to force-generating events. Our experiments also indicated that an asymmetric, polarized rate of dynein binding to microtubules causes the force imbalance that positions the spindle. GPR-1/2 increased both the overall dynein density and its residence time, or pulling processivity, although the residence time was not polarized.
